Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Vulnerable HAPI FHIR org.hl7.fhir.utilities < 6.9.10 in software inventory (CVE-2026-55471) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

HAPI FHIR XXE: DOCTYPE/ENTITY SYSTEM payload posted to FHIR endpoint (CVE-2026-55471) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POST/PUT to FHIR API paths whose XML body carries XXE markers (<!DOCTYPE … <!ENTITY … SYSTEM 'file://' or 'http://'). Targets the entry-point of CVE-2026-55471 where attacker-controlled XML is fed to XsltUtilities.saxonTransform with an unhardened Saxon TransformerFactory. Rationale: Article specifies the entry point is XML fed to XsltUtilities.saxonTransform; PoC literally shows '<!DOCTYPE root [' + '<!ENTITY canary SYSTEM "file://..."' + '<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://..."'. FHIR URL fragments come from standard HAPI deployments. Corroborated via vulnerability.circl.lu GHSA-2F55-G35J-5JMF entry. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Burp/ZAP/Nuclei scans hitting FHIR endpoints with XXE payloads as part of authorized AppSec testing
  • Legitimate FHIR XML payloads that include a benign internal DOCTYPE (rare but possible for IG packages)
  • Health-IT interop tools that embed XSD references via DOCTYPE during conformance testing
  • WAF echo-back / debug logs that quote the original payload back into the log line
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Burp","ZAP","Nuclei","sqlmap","Acunetix") and SourceIP !in ("<known_scanner_ips>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Pull the full request body and confirm an external SYSTEM identifier (file://, http://, https://, jar:, netdoc:). Map the destination FHIR endpoint to its backing JVM/container and check whether HAPI FHIR org.hl7.fhir.utilities < 6.9.10 is present. 2) CONTAIN — Block the source IP at the WAF, drop any in-flight session, and add a virtual patch rule that rejects FHIR POST/PUT bodies containing <!DOCTYPE or <!ENTITY. If exploitation confirmed, isolate the FHIR app server and rotate any local secrets the JVM could read. 3) HUNT — Pivot on the source IP across the last 30d for other FHIR endpoints and parameter-entity variants (UC2). Pull DeviceFileEvents on the JVM host for /etc/passwd, application.properties, ~/.aws/credentials reads (UC3). Pull DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound HTTP/DNS from java.exe to the attacker-controlled OOB domain (UC4).
// Defender XDR does not capture HTTP request bodies; pivot is the FHIR endpoint URL hit (DeviceNetworkEvents shows the host:port + URL fragment only). Pair with WAF logs in Sentinel (sentinel_kql below) for body inspection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted" or ActionType == "ConnectionInbound"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/fhir/","/hl7/fhir/","/baseR4/","/baseDstu3/","/StructureDefinition","/ValueSet")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat.exe","tomcat9.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
let FhirPaths = dynamic(["/fhir/","/hl7/fhir/","/baseR4/","/baseDstu3/","/StructureDefinition","/ValueSet","/metadata"]);
let XxeMarkers = dynamic(["<!DOCTYPE","<!ENTITY","SYSTEM \"file:","SYSTEM \"http:","SYSTEM 'file:","SYSTEM 'http:"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT")
| where RequestURL has_any (FhirPaths)
| extend BodyCandidates = strcat(tostring(DeviceCustomString1), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString2), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString3), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString4), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString5), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString6), "|", tostring(RequestContext), "|", tostring(Message))
| where BodyCandidates has_any (XxeMarkers)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, BodyExcerpt = substring(BodyCandidates, 0, 1024), DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: HAPI FHIR XXE Payload in HTTP Body (CVE-2026-55471)
id: 8e2a0c14-9e7f-4d5a-bf3e-5471a55471aa
status: experimental
description: Detects inbound HTTP POST/PUT to FHIR endpoints whose body contains XML External Entity declarations, the entry vector for CVE-2026-55471 in HAPI FHIR XsltUtilities.saxonTransform.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf
  - https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_method:
    cs-method:
      - POST
      - PUT
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/fhir/'
      - '/hl7/fhir/'
      - '/baseR4/'
      - '/baseDstu3/'
      - '/StructureDefinition'
      - '/ValueSet'
  selection_body:
    cs-body|contains:
      - '<!DOCTYPE'
      - '<!ENTITY'
      - 'SYSTEM "file:'
      - 'SYSTEM "http:'
  condition: selection_method and selection_path and selection_body
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate FHIR clients using internal DTDs (rare in modern FHIR XML)
  - Security scanners (Burp, ZAP, Nuclei) testing the same endpoints
level: high
(@http.method:(POST OR PUT)) (@http.url_details.path:(*\/fhir\/* OR *\/hl7\/fhir\/* OR *\/baseR4\/* OR *\/baseDstu3\/* OR *\/StructureDefinition* OR *\/ValueSet*)) (@http.request.body:(*"<!DOCTYPE"* OR *"<!ENTITY"* OR *"SYSTEM \"file:"* OR *"SYSTEM \"http:"*))
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method in ("POST","PUT") (Web.url="*/fhir/*" OR Web.url="*/hl7/fhir/*" OR Web.url="*/baseR4/*" OR Web.url="*/baseDstu3/*" OR Web.url="*/StructureDefinition*" OR Web.url="*/ValueSet*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.user Web.http_user_agent _raw | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | search _raw="*<!DOCTYPE*" OR _raw="*<!ENTITY*SYSTEM*" | rex field=_raw "(?i)(?<xxe_marker><!ENTITY[^>]+SYSTEM\s+[\"'](?:file|http|https|ftp|jar|netdoc|gopher):[^\"']+[\"'])" | where isnotnull(xxe_marker) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method in ("POST","PUT") (Web.url="*/fhir/*" OR Web.url="*/hl7/fhir/*" OR Web.url="*/baseR4/*" OR Web.url="*/baseDstu3/*" OR Web.url="*/StructureDefinition*" OR Web.url="*/ValueSet*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.user Web.http_user_agent _raw | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | search _raw="*<!DOCTYPE*" OR _raw="*<!ENTITY*SYSTEM*" | rex field=_raw "(?i)(?<xxe_marker><!ENTITY[^>]+SYSTEM\s+[\"'](?:file|http|https|ftp|jar|netdoc|gopher):[^\"']+[\"'])" | where isnotnull(xxe_marker) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
HAPI FHIR XXE: parameter-entity (<!ENTITY %) OOB exfil pattern on FHIR endpoint AIExploitation High
Higher-fidelity sibling of the generic DOCTYPE hunt: matches only payloads that declare a parameter entity (<!ENTITY %) with an external SYSTEM identifier, the exact pattern used for blind XXE / SSRF in the article's PoC. Parameter entities are vanishingly rare in benign FHIR traffic. Rationale: Article's PoC uses `<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://127.0.0.1:port/evil-fhir-xslt-ssrf.dtd">` to set up OOB exfil — the parameter-entity construct (`%`) is the distinguishing signature of XXE-via-DTD attacks and almost never appears in legitimate FHIR XML. Much lower-FP than UC1's generic DOCTYPE/ENTITY hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized AppSec scanning by internal red team / Burp Pro extensions
  • Bug-bounty researcher probing exposed FHIR test environments
  • FHIR conformance test harnesses that embed parameter entities in edge-case test vectors (extremely rare)
  • Researcher proof-of-concepts in pre-prod where the source IP belongs to an internal pentest range
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<internal_appsec_scanner_ips>") and RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Burp","ZAP","Nuclei","sqlmap")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — This signature is high-fidelity; treat any hit as exploitation attempt until proven otherwise. Capture the full Body, the source IP, the targeted FHIR resource path, and the parent JVM hostname. Confirm HAPI FHIR version on the receiver. 2) CONTAIN — Block source IP at WAF immediately. Apply ModSecurity / WAF rule to drop any inbound XML containing `<!ENTITY %` for FHIR endpoints regardless of upgrade status. Snapshot the JVM heap if exploit may have succeeded so artefacts can be retrieved later. 3) HUNT — Pivot to UC4 (java.exe outbound to the OOB callback domain in the SYSTEM URI) and UC3 (java.exe reading sensitive local files). Search the WAF for the same source IP over 30d on any FHIR-shaped path. Cross-check the OOB host/IP against threat-intel feeds and add to the Sentinel ThreatIntelligenceIndicator table.
// Defender XDR has no HTTP body visibility; this detection lives in WAF/proxy logs surfaced through Sentinel. The Defender query below is the host-side companion: JVM serving FHIR that immediately performs an outbound HTTP fetch to a public IP (the parameter-entity callback).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hapi","org.hl7.fhir","tomcat","jetty","spring-boot","wildfly")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let FhirPaths = dynamic(["/fhir/","/hl7/fhir/","/baseR4/","/baseDstu3/","/StructureDefinition","/ValueSet","/metadata"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT")
| where RequestURL has_any (FhirPaths)
| extend Body = strcat(tostring(DeviceCustomString1),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString2),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString3),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString4),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString5),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString6),"|",tostring(RequestContext),"|",tostring(Message))
| where Body matches regex @"(?i)<!ENTITY\s+%\s+\w+\s+SYSTEM\s+[""'](?:file|http|https|ftp|jar|netdoc|gopher):"
| extend ParamEntity = extract(@"(?i)(<!ENTITY\s+%\s+\w+\s+SYSTEM\s+[""'][^""']+[""'])", 1, Body)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, ParamEntity, BodyExcerpt = substring(Body, 0, 1024)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JVM serving HAPI FHIR reads sensitive local files (XXE file:// disclosure) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects post-exploitation file reads by the JVM hosting HAPI FHIR: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/hosts, application.properties, application.yml, cloud credentials, and Kubernetes secrets. Catches the file:// SYSTEM-entity arm of CVE-2026-55471 regardless of whether the inbound WAF caught the payload. Rationale: Article's PoC uses `<!ENTITY canary SYSTEM "file://...">` to read a temp file containing `TOP-SECRET-FHIR-XSLT-CANARY-3f9a17c2`. Real attackers will pivot to /etc/passwd, application.properties (DB creds), and cloud-credential files. JVM as the reader + Java-app-server cmdline narrows scope. Corroborated against vulnerability.circl.lu confirmation of the file-disclosure exploitation primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1005 T1083 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • HAPI FHIR legitimately loading its own application.yml / hapi.properties from its install directory at startup
  • Spring Boot Actuator config refresh reading application config
  • Backup/snapshot tooling that crawls the FHIR app directory and triggers file-access events on config
  • Sysadmin running diagnostic tools (strace, jstack against the JVM) that incidentally surface as the JVM touching these files
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath endswith "hapi.properties" and FolderPath startswith "/opt/hapi-fhir/") and not (FolderPath endswith "application.yml" and FolderPath has "/conf/")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Confirm the JVM in question is the FHIR app server (check parent process tree, listening ports, classpath). Pull the timestamp of the file read and look ±60s in CommonSecurityLog / Web datamodel for an inbound POST/PUT to a FHIR endpoint (UC1/UC2). 2) CONTAIN — Stop the JVM, snapshot heap + thread dump, isolate the host from network. Rotate every secret the JVM could read (application.properties DB creds, AWS access keys, K8s service-account tokens, SSH keys). 3) HUNT — Run UC4 to look for OOB exfil of the file contents to attacker-controlled domains. Search the same JVM hosts for inbound traffic to FHIR endpoints from the source IP over the past 30d. Apply the WAF virtual-patch from UC2 to every FHIR-fronting WAF.

description: Java process running HAPI FHIR / a typical Java app server reads sensitive local files (passwd, shadow, application config, cloud creds). Likely XXE file:// disclosure via CVE-2026-55471 if no admin justification exists.

HAPI FHIR JVM out-of-band callback to non-corporate destination (XXE OOB exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the SSRF / blind-XXE arm of CVE-2026-55471: the FHIR-serving JVM makes an outbound HTTP fetch or DNS lookup to a public destination it has never previously contacted, immediately after an inbound POST/PUT to a FHIR endpoint. Captures both the parameter-entity DTD fetch and the file-content exfil pattern. Rationale: PoC sets up `<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://127.0.0.1:port/evil-fhir-xslt-ssrf.dtd">` and the JVM resolves it, generating an outbound HTTP request from the Saxon TransformerFactory. Real attackers replace 127.0.0.1 with attacker.com. Anti-join against 30d baseline turns 'JVM made an HTTP request' into 'JVM contacted a destination it never contacted before'. Corroborated against vulnerability.circl.lu confirmation of SSRF primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1071.004 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • HAPI FHIR pulling new external IG (Implementation Guide) packages from a registry (registry.fhir.org, packages.simplifier.net)
  • JVM auto-update / Maven Central / Spring Boot Actuator phoning home
  • Newly-onboarded healthcare partner whose endpoint URL is genuinely contacted for the first time
  • Container image rebuilds that change the destination set seen at runtime
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("registry.fhir.org","packages.simplifier.net","packages2.fhir.org","repo.maven.apache.org","repo1.maven.org","jcenter.bintray.com"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Confirm the destination domain/IP is not a known FHIR registry (registry.fhir.org, packages.simplifier.net, packages2.fhir.org). Look at the immediate-prior inbound HTTP requests to the JVM (CommonSecurityLog / W3CIISLog within 60s before the outbound) for FHIR endpoint POST/PUT carrying the matching attacker domain in a SYSTEM identifier. 2) CONTAIN — If the destination is an attacker callback, block it at egress firewall + add to ThreatIntelligenceIndicator. Rotate any secrets that may have been leaked over the channel (assume worst case — UC3 enumerates targets). 3) HUNT — Pivot on the attacker destination across all JVM hosts in the estate over the past 30d. Pull the file-read events from UC3 in the same time window. Check whether the attacker domain appears in DNS logs from other hosts (lateral targeting).

Vulnerable HAPI FHIR org.hl7.fhir.utilities < 6.9.10 in software inventory (CVE-2026-55471) AIReconnaissance High
Inventory pivot: lists every host running HAPI FHIR with the vulnerable org.hl7.fhir.utilities Maven artifact (< 6.9.10). Drives patching and tells the SOC which hosts to prioritise for the runtime detections (UC1-UC4) until upgraded. Rationale: Article pins the vulnerable artifact (`ca.uhn.hapi.fhir:org.hl7.fhir.utilities`) and the vulnerable file:line (XsltUtilities.java:61/91/106 in <= 6.9.8). Web search confirmed the fix landed in 6.9.10, so the vulnerable range is < 6.9.10. CveId match is the cleanest inventory pivot and directly drives patch prioritisation + scopes UC1-UC4 to the right hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Test / lab hosts intentionally running old HAPI FHIR for compatibility testing
  • Containers pinned to a vulnerable version because of an unrelated downstream dependency conflict — true positive for inventory but not actionable until refactor
  • TVM lag — DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities may not enumerate Java JARs unless the agent indexes them; results may under-report
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Confirm the host is actually serving FHIR (listening on a FHIR endpoint, not just a build artifact). Capture HAPI FHIR base version + org.hl7.fhir.utilities version. 2) CONTAIN — For internet-facing FHIR hosts: deploy the UC2 WAF rule (block `<!ENTITY %`) as virtual patch. Schedule emergency upgrade to org.hl7.fhir.utilities >= 6.9.10. 3) HUNT — Enable UC1-UC4 with elevated priority for the listed hosts. Backsearch CommonSecurityLog 30d for any FHIR POST/PUT with XXE markers targeting these hosts. Pull DeviceFileEvents for any sensitive-file read by their JVM (UC3).

Anomalous POST volume to Langflow /api/v1/upload/{flow_id} (CVE-2026-55450) AIDelivery High
Detects exploitation of the deprecated unauthenticated upload endpoint by counting POST requests and aggregate request-body bytes per source IP toward the Langflow web tier (default TCP 7860). The advisory confirms no auth, no size limit, and an absolute-path information leak in every response — so a spike to this exact URI from a non-baseline source is article-specific high signal. Rationale: Article gives exact URI '/api/v1/upload/{flow_id}', POST method, default port 7860, and 'no limitations' on size. CIM Web tstats threshold on POST count + bytes_in surfaces both burst and single-large-file attacks; Defender / Falcon use port-7860 connection counts as a fallback since they lack HTTP URI visibility.
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or CI/CD pipeline bulk-uploading flow assets during a model migration
  • Internal load test against the deprecated /upload endpoint pre-1.9.1
  • Integration partner re-uploading flows via the legacy endpoint before customer cutover to 1.9.1
  • Langflow itself replaying queued uploads after a restart or backup restore
  • Internal scanner (Nuclei/Tenable) PoC-checking CVE-2026-55450 against a known host
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<cicd_ip_1>", "<internal_scanner_ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm Langflow version (<1.9.1 is vulnerable; fix is PR #12831). Check source IP against CI/CD allowlist, validate whether it's an internal scanner. Sum bytes uploaded vs free disk on the host. 2) Contain — block the source IP at the WAF / perimeter, gate /api/v1/upload/* behind an authenticated WAF rule, restart Langflow if disk pressure is degrading service, purge unauthorized files under <cache>/langflow/<flow_id>/. 3) Hunt — pivot on the source IP across all Langflow URIs (other deprecated endpoints may also be unauth); cross-check with UC2/UC3 cache writes; review identity logs for any later legitimate access from the same IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where LocalPort == 7860
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback","Private")
| summarize Conns = count(), Hosts = dcount(DeviceName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where Conns > 50
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/upload/"
| summarize Posts = count(), TotalBytes = sum(toint(ReceivedBytes)), Statuses = make_set(EventOutcome) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Posts > 20 or TotalBytes > 1073741824
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(nginx OR apache OR iis OR caddy OR azure.appservices) @http.method:POST @http.url_details.path:*/api/v1/upload/*
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 LocalPort=7860
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count(as=conns))

File-write storm in Langflow cache directory (CVE-2026-55450 disk exhaustion) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the impact stage of CVE-2026-55450 — a flood of attacker-controlled files written under the Langflow cache directory using the PoC-confirmed naming layout '<cache>/langflow/<flow_uuid>/<sha256-hex>.<ext>'. Thresholded on file count and total bytes so it fires on disk-exhaustion attempts, not on normal flow saves. Rationale: PoC response exposes the canonical cache path '/Users/ori/Library/Caches/langflow/<flow_id>/<sha256>.txt' — the SHA256-hex filename + per-flow-uuid layout is the same on every OS (platformdirs). The regex anchors filename = 32+ char hex (Langflow's content-hash naming) under a *langflow* parent, so it only fires on the upload code path, not on legitimate model/asset writes elsewhere on disk.
ATT&CKT1499.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator bulk-loading a real corpus of flows post-upgrade to 1.9.1 (legit auth'd uploads still write to the same path layout)
  • Backup-restore agent replaying cache files after a Langflow recovery
  • Cluster sync replicating cache content to a new pod or node
  • Container image build copying baked-in flow fixtures into the cache during startup
  • Langflow upgrade script regenerating cache content for migrated flows
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.exe", "rsync", "backupd", "restic")
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm the writing process is the Langflow server (uvicorn/python) and not a backup/sync agent; check disk-free on host; sample a few SHA256 filenames and confirm they exist via 'ls /<cache>/langflow/<flow_id>/<sha>.*'; cross-reference Timestamp with web logs for matching POSTs (see UC3). 2) Contain — stop Langflow if disk free <10%, purge unauthorized cache files (DO NOT bulk-delete /langflow/ — it also holds legitimate state, target by flow_id of unknown ownership only), block the source IP at WAF. 3) Hunt — query Web/CommonSecurityLog for /api/v1/upload/{flow_id} POSTs landing on this host in the same window; check whether file-creation continued post-block (proxy bypass / multi-source attack); inventory Langflow versions org-wide via TVM.

| where FolderPath has_any ("/langflow/", @"\langflow\", "Caches/langflow", ".cache/langflow")
| where FileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{32,}\."
| summarize FileCount = count(), TotalBytes = sum(FileSize), SampleFile = any(FileName), SampleFolder = any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where FileCount > 50 or TotalBytes > 5368709120
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/langflow/", "\\langflow\\", "Caches/langflow", ".cache/langflow")
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{32,}\."
| summarize FileCount = count(), TotalBytes = sum(toint(TargetFileSize)), SamplePath = any(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FileCount > 50 or TotalBytes > 5368709120
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(linux.auditd OR windows.sysmon) (@TargetFilename:(*\/langflow\/* OR *\\langflow\\* OR *\/Caches\/langflow\/* OR *\/.cache\/langflow\/*) OR @file.path:*langflow*)

Correlation: Langflow /api/v1/upload POST + cache file-creation spike (CVE-2026-55450) AIActions on Objectives High
Joins web access logs (POST to /api/v1/upload/) with filesystem events writing into the Langflow cache directory within the same 5-minute window — confirms the full attack chain (request → on-disk impact) and rules out unrelated cache growth from model loads, replicas, or backups. High-confidence variant for paging. Rationale: Per reviewer feedback #2 — UC1 and UC2 each have residual FP risk (legit bulk uploads can trip either alone), but the join collapses that to near zero: only a host that receives the unauthenticated POSTs AND writes the matching SHA256-named cache files in the same 5-minute bucket survives. Time-window correlation as per the KB pattern-time-window-correlation.

Data sourcesWeb Endpoint.Filesystem

  • Backup restore that simultaneously serves API and replays cache files
  • Blue-team validation run that PoCs CVE-2026-55450 on a known host
Response runbook

Confirm Langflow version is <1.9.1. 2) Contain — block source IPs from the Posts side at the WAF, gate the endpoint behind auth, free disk if under pressure, purge unauthorized flow_id directories. 3) Hunt — extend the join across the past 7d for any prior persistent abuser from the same /24; sweep TVM for vulnerable Langflow installs (<1.9.1) and prioritize internet-facing first; check whether response status was 201 (info leak occurred) on every survived row.

Vulnerable Langflow exposed to network (CVE-2026-55450 inventory) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces Langflow installations on tenant hosts with version <1.9.1 — the affected range per the GHSA — joined with DeviceInfo IsInternetFacing, so SOC can prioritise patching internet-reachable hosts before the exploitation UCs fire. Pre-exploit hygiene hunt. Rationale: Article gives the exact affected range (langflow <1.9.1) and CVE ID. TVM tables surface the vulnerable software inventory; joining DeviceInfo's IsInternetFacing gives SOC an immediate patch-priority list. Pre-exploit hunt, no attack telemetry required — the right place to start before the alerting UCs fire.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow installed in a dev/test environment that's not actually exposed despite the IsInternetFacing flag (offline namespace)
  • Custom Langflow fork named 'langflow' but maintained internally with the patch backported
  • Stale TVM data — host was patched but inventory hasn't refreshed yet
  • Air-gapped lab host where the version string is intentionally left at <1.9.1
  • Pre-1.9.1 install on a host that's only reachable from a private VPC despite the IP being public-class
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.9.1" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.9.2" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.10"
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm SoftwareVersion is genuinely <1.9.1 (string comparison can lie on pre-release tags like 1.9.0rc1); confirm IsInternetFacing by checking the public IP listens on TCP 7860 from outside. 2) Contain — coordinate with the platform owner to upgrade to 1.9.1 (fix is PR #12831); if upgrade can't happen same day, gate /api/v1/upload/* behind auth at the WAF or remove external exposure. 3) Hunt — pivot to UC1/UC2/UC3 historical search for any prior exploitation on the same hosts; check Langflow API access logs for prior anonymous POSTs to /api/v1/upload/ that would indicate the gap was already used.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-55450" or (SoftwareName =~ "langflow" and SoftwareVendor in~ ("langflow-ai", "langflow"))
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId
  ) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-55450" or SoftwareName =~ "langflow"
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId
  ) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
| order by IsInternetFacing desc

Actions on Objectives

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crypto Clipper Campaign Abuses Fake Reviews, AI Narrators, and VirusTotal Comments

The Hacker News
2026-06-17 8 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An unknown threat actor has been observed leveraging paid or promoted posts on legitimate news websites to drum up buzz for their warez, according to new findings from Check Point Research. The threat actor also has at their disposal a dedicated WordPress phishing page that acts as the central hub, alongside GitHub and SourceForge projects promoted by fake accounts, a YouTube channel, and a

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Crypto 'sniper bot' / Aviator Predictor lure download-and-execute from SourceForge or GitHub · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Crypto 'sniper bot' / Aviator Predictor lure download-and-execute from SourceForge or GitHub AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Check Point Rust clipper campaign by correlating downloads of executables from SourceForge or GitHub whose filenames match the campaign's specific social-engineering lures (Solana/Pump.fun sniper bots, Aviator Predictor, crash-game predictors) with subsequent first execution from a user-writable path. The SHA256 join between the file-drop and process-execution events makes this article-specific rather than catching any crypto-themed tool a user happens to run. Rationale: The article explicitly names Solana sniper bots, Pump.fun sniper bots, Aviator Predictor, and crash-game predictors as the lure themes, with SourceForge and GitHub as the named distribution platforms — the FileOriginUrl + lure-token correlation ties endpoint detection back to the campaign's specific social-engineering hooks. Cross-checked The Hacker News and InfotechLead coverage and the clip.gif demo (showing the Notepad btc_wallet → wallet-app clipboard substitution) for behavioral confirmation; no public SHA256/wallet IOCs were available at search time, so this is a hunting-tier behavioral query. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/crypto-clipper-campaign-abuses-fake.html • https://infotechlead.com/security/cybercriminals-manipulate-github-youtube-and-virustotal-to-spread-crypto-stealing-malware-96613 • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi-BtcZtH5fovAmDU_naao6gUXxP7z2gbzRS5dh0ihlwxmyvrKEOvVzkGwCndKLmeurQQ9gVebjrJynRkx8dJF858sS7Xqk9OL4diFcjia9zgBeRndSjrH6j_uuPTEzs2izOhZlS6FeCjtZV8IxCw96vTn1CUIx4nLOfpW7Y1FiRvtSdWovorzSgeK5FZfz/s1700-e365/clip.gif
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1608.001 T1583.006 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crypto-savvy developer running a legitimate open-source Solana sniper bot from GitHub for personal trading
  • Malware analyst or threat researcher detonating a known crypto-clipper sample in a triage VM
  • Sports betting / fantasy analytics desktop tools whose filename literally contains 'predictor' (e.g. 'NFLPredictor.exe')
  • Game-development AI utilities packaged with names like 'CrashPredictor' for in-game economy testing
  • Red-team / purple-team engagement deliberately running the same campaign tooling for detection tuning
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe", "explorer.exe") and FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\")) and not (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName in~ ("Microsoft Corporation", "Google LLC", "Mozilla Corporation", "Valve"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the SHA256 from the join and submit to VirusTotal + MalwareBazaar; verify FileOriginUrl resolves to a SourceForge project or GitHub repo with the boosted-but-shallow signals Check Point flagged (very recent commits, single-contributor, fake-looking stars). Ask the user via chat whether they intentionally downloaded a crypto trading or gambling tool. 2) Contain: Isolate the device in Defender/Falcon. Block the SHA256 organisation-wide via custom IOC. Force-reset any crypto wallet credentials the user used on that device and warn the user not to copy-paste wallet addresses until the host is rebuilt — the clipper substitutes addresses silently. 3) Hunt: Pivot org-wide on the SHA256 and the FileOriginUrl host; expand the lure-token regex to scan 60 days of DeviceFileEvents for sibling drops; check DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound HTTPS from the binary to the SourceForge/GitHub origin in case of an updater channel.
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let LureTokens = dynamic(["sniper","pumpfun","pump.fun","aviator","predictor","solana-bot","solanabot","crash-predictor","crashpredictor"]);
let SuspectOriginHosts = dynamic(["sourceforge.net","sf.net","github.com","github.io","githubusercontent.com","raw.githubusercontent.com"]);
let SuspectDrops = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ActionType == "FileCreated"
    | where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".msi" or FileName endswith ".zip" or FileName endswith ".dmg" or FileName endswith ".pkg" or FileName endswith ".app"
    | where isnotempty(FileOriginUrl)
    | where tolower(FileOriginUrl) has_any (SuspectOriginHosts)
    | extend NameLower = tolower(FileName)
    | where NameLower has_any (LureTokens)
    | project DropTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, DroppedFolder = FolderPath, DroppedName = FileName, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", "/Users/", "/Applications/", "/tmp/")
| join kind=inner SuspectDrops on $left.DeviceId == $right.DeviceId, $left.SHA256 == $right.SHA256
| where Timestamp >= DropTime
| extend DelayMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, DropTime)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, DropTime, DelayMinutes, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let LureRegex = @"(?i)(sniper|pump[\.\-_]?fun|aviator|predictor|solana[\-_]?bot|crash[\-_]?predictor)";
let UserPathRegex = @"(?i)\\(Users|Downloads|AppData|Public|Temp)\\";
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetProcessName matches regex LureRegex
| where TargetProcessName matches regex UserPathRegex
| where TargetProcessName endswith ".exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/crypto-clipper-campaign-abuses-fake.html

  category: process_creation

  selection_name:
    Image|contains:
      - 'sniper'
      - 'pumpfun'
      - 'pump.fun'
      - 'aviator'
      - 'predictor'
      - 'solana-bot'
      - 'solanabot'
      - 'crash-predictor'

| ImageFileName=/\\(Users|Downloads|AppData|Public|Temp)\\/i
| ImageFileName=/\.exe$/i
| UserName!=/\$$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, SHA256HashData], function=[count(), min(@timestamp, as=FirstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=LastSeen), collect([CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])])

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] wscript/cscript executing .vbs from user staging folder (Poisson VBScript stager)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Junior Hacker Used Tailscale and OpenSSH to Keep Access After His C2 Went Offlin
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OpenSSH Server install on Windows workstation (Poisson persistence pivot) · [LLM] Logon-trigger scheduled task at HIGHEST privileges launching script interpreter · [LLM] authorized_keys file write on Windows host (SSH key persistence) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Tailscale client install or tailnet connection (100.100.100.0/8 / login.tailscale.com) · [LLM] SSH reverse tunnel (ssh -R) outbound from Windows endpoint · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] powercfg disabling standby/hibernate to keep host harvest-ready · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change
OpenSSH Server install on Windows workstation (Poisson persistence pivot) AIInstallation High
Detects Add-WindowsCapability adding the OpenSSH.Server feature, sshd.exe service start, or registry/firewall configuration enabling sshd on a Windows endpoint. Article-specific: Poisson installed OpenSSH on April 7 as a C2-independent reentry path so access survived the Havoc takedown. Rationale: Cato's first hunt-list item is literally 'OpenSSH Server installs on a Windows workstation, which is rarely legitimate.' Defender ships OpenSSH as a FoD capability — Add-WindowsCapability/dism/sshd.exe are the three install vectors; combining them with non-machine accounts keeps this near-zero FP.
ATT&CKT1133 T1021.004 T1505
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dev/SRE workstation where the user genuinely needs sshd to test Ansible/Terraform from WSL
  • IT pilot enabling RemoteSSH for management at scale
  • Visual Studio Code 'Remote-SSH' setup wizard installing the OpenSSH client (not server)
  • Lab/test image being provisioned by Packer
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("MsiExec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe") and AccountName !in~ ("SYSTEM","LOCAL SERVICE","NETWORK SERVICE")
Response runbook
Triage: pivot on the host's last 24h DeviceProcessEvents — look for VBS->PowerShell->.NET chain (Havoc Demon staging), Tailscale process, RustDesk install, schtasks /Create at logon, and any keylogger artifact under user staging dirs. Check DeviceLogonEvents for new inbound RemoteInteractive logons after install. Contain: stop the sshd service, disable the OpenSSH.Server capability, remove host firewall allow rule for TCP/22, block egress to login.tailscale.com and DuckDNS at edge, isolate the host. Hunt: across the org, query for tailscale.exe execution, ssh.exe with -R flag, schtasks /RL HIGHEST /SC ONLOGON launching script interpreters, and powercfg standby-timeout-* 0 over the same 30d window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Add-WindowsCapability","OpenSSH.Server","Start-Service sshd","Set-Service -Name sshd"))
   or (FileName =~ "dism.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "OpenSSH")
   or FileName =~ "sshd.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where AccountType =~ "User"
| where (NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("Add-WindowsCapability","OpenSSH.Server","Start-Service sshd"))
   or (NewProcessName endswith @"\dism.exe" and CommandLine has "OpenSSH")
   or NewProcessName endswith @"\sshd.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OpenSSH Server Capability Install on Windows Workstation
id: a7d2e9c4-3f8b-4f1a-9b6e-2c5d8e7f1a4b
description: Detects installation/start of OpenSSH Server feature on a Windows endpoint, as used by 'Poisson' for a C2-independent reentry path.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/junior-hacker-used-tailscale-and.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.t1133
  - attack.t1021.004
  - attack.t1505
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_addcap:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\dism.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'Add-WindowsCapability'
      - 'OpenSSH.Server'
      - 'Start-Service sshd'
      - 'Set-Service -Name sshd'
  selection_sshd:
    Image|endswith: '\sshd.exe'
  condition: 1 of selection_*
level: high
source:(windows.security OR windows.sysmon) ((@Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\dism.exe OR *\DISM.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*Add-WindowsCapability* OR *OpenSSH.Server* OR *"Start-Service sshd"*)) OR @Image:(*\sshd.exe OR *\SSHD.EXE))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName=/\\sshd\.exe$/i OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|dism)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/(Add-WindowsCapability|OpenSSH\.Server|Start-Service\s+sshd)/i)) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe) AND (Processes.process="*Add-WindowsCapability*OpenSSH.Server*" OR Processes.process="*Set-Service*sshd*Automatic*" OR Processes.process="*Start-Service*sshd*") OR Processes.process_name=sshd.exe OR (Processes.process_name=dism.exe AND Processes.process="*OpenSSH*") by host Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.process_name=pwsh.exe) AND (Processes.process="*Add-WindowsCapability*OpenSSH.Server*" OR Processes.process="*Set-Service*sshd*Automatic*" OR Processes.process="*Start-Service*sshd*") OR Processes.process_name=sshd.exe OR (Processes.process_name=dism.exe AND Processes.process="*OpenSSH*") by host Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | sort - firstTime
Tailscale client install or tailnet connection (100.100.100.0/8 / login.tailscale.com) AICommand & Control High
Surfaces tailscale.exe/tailscaled.exe execution, tailscale-up commands, DNS for login.tailscale.com, or any traffic into the 100.64.0.0/10 CGNAT / 100.100.100.0/24 magic-DNS range. Article-specific: Poisson joined victim machines to his private tailnet for a fully out-of-band reentry path that survived the Havoc takedown. Rationale: Cato names Tailscale outright as Poisson's 'separate door' and the article gives the magic-DNS IP 100.100.100.2 and login.tailscale.com as pivot indicators. The detection joins process telemetry (tailscale.exe/up/login) and network telemetry (100.100.100/24, port 41641, control-plane DNS) so it catches the install AND the active tunnel.
ATT&CKT1572 T1219 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineering team using Tailscale as their official corporate VPN
  • Remote SRE accessing infra over a documented tailnet
  • Personal Tailscale install on a BYOD/AAD-registered laptop that's also on the corp tenant
  • Tailscale being silently bundled by another tool like Headscale or NextDNS
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in (dynamic(["<approved-tailscale-hosts>"])) and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("SYSTEM","<corp-IT-deployment-account>")
Response runbook
Triage: confirm whether the host is in IT's Tailscale-approved inventory; if not, pull DeviceProcessEvents 24h before/after the install for a Havoc/RustDesk staging chain and check DeviceLogonEvents for inbound RemoteInteractive over 100.x.x.x. Contain: kill tailscaled, uninstall the package, block login.tailscale.com + controlplane.tailscale.com + derp*.tailscale.com at proxy, deny 100.64.0.0/10 egress at edge, revoke the tailnet auth key if obtainable. Hunt: pivot org-wide for any host that resolved login.tailscale.com over the past 90d but is not on the approved list; correlate with OpenSSH installs and powercfg standby changes on the same host.
let TS_Proc = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("tailscale.exe","tailscaled.exe")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has_any (" up --authkey"," up --login-server","tailscale login","tailscale up") and ProcessCommandLine has "tailscale")
   or FolderPath has @"\Tailscale\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName;
let TS_Net = DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("login.tailscale.com","controlplane.tailscale.com","derp.tailscale.com")
   or RemoteIP startswith "100.100.100."
   or (RemotePort == 41641 and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
union isfuzzy=true TS_Proc, TS_Net
| order by Timestamp desc
let TS_Proc = SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\tailscale.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\tailscaled.exe" or CommandLine has_any ("tailscale up","tailscale login","--authkey")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName;
let TS_Net = DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Name has_any ("login.tailscale.com","controlplane.tailscale.com","derp")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name;
union isfuzzy=true TS_Proc, TS_Net
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: b8e3facd-4f9c-4f2b-ac7f-3d6e9f8a2b5c
description: Detects tailscale.exe/tailscaled.exe execution or tailnet bootstrap commands on a Windows endpoint, per Cato CTRL's hunt for 'Poisson's' Tailscale fallback channel.
references:

| tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=tailscale.exe OR Processes.process_name=tailscaled.exe OR Processes.process="*tailscale*up*" OR Processes.process="*tailscale*login*") by host Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | append [| tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip=100.64.0.0/10 OR All_Traffic.dest="login.tailscale.com" OR All_Traffic.dest="controlplane.tailscale.com" OR All_Traffic.dest_port=41641 by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`] | sort - count

SSH reverse tunnel (ssh -R) outbound from Windows endpoint AICommand & Control High
Detects ssh.exe invoked with `-R <port>` (remote-port-forward) to an external host — the technique Poisson used to expose victim ports back through his SSH listener. Tier alerting because ssh.exe with -R on a workstation is overwhelmingly attacker tradecraft. Rationale: Cato's hunt list calls out 'ssh -R reverse tunnels heading to outside hosts' verbatim. The regex `-R <bind>:<port>` keys on Poisson's actual SSH-listener setup; pairing with `AccountName !endswith "$"` and `ssh.exe` on a workstation (vs. server) keeps the FP cone tight.
ATT&CKT1572 T1021.004 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using ngrok-style SSH reverse tunnel to expose a local dev server
  • DevOps engineer port-forwarding through a bastion for debugging
  • GitHub Actions self-hosted runner setup script
  • Educational SSH tutorial run by a curious user
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("code.exe","WindowsTerminal.exe","git-bash.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "DEV-"
Response runbook
Triage: extract the destination from `ReverseSpec` — passive-DNS / WHOIS / abuse.ch checks on the bind host; pull DeviceNetworkEvents from that host for the same time window. Contain: kill the ssh.exe process tree, block the destination IP at egress, rotate any private keys cached in %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\ on the host. Hunt: cross-org search for ssh.exe -R, OpenSSH server installs, and Tailscale activations on the same host within 30 days — Poisson chained all three.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "ssh.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(^|\s)-R\s+(\S*:)?\d{1,5}(:[^\s]+:\d{1,5})?"
| extend ReverseSpec = extract(@"(?i)(?:^|\s)-R\s+(\S+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, ReverseSpec, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where AccountType =~ "User"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\ssh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(^|\s)-R\s+(\S*:)?\d{1,5}"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SSH Reverse Tunnel Outbound from Windows Endpoint

  condition: selection
level: high
source:(windows.security OR windows.sysmon) @Image:(*\ssh.exe OR *\SSH.EXE OR *\Ssh.exe) @CommandLine:(*" -R "* OR *" -R3"* OR *" -R 1"* OR *" -R 2"* OR *" -R 4"* OR *" -R 5"* OR *" -R 6"* OR *" -R 7"* OR *" -R 8"* OR *" -R 9"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\ssh\.exe$/i CommandLine=/(^|\s)-R\s+(\S*:)?\d{1,5}/ | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())

wscript/cscript executing .vbs from user staging folder (Poisson VBScript stager) AIDelivery High
Detects wscript.exe or cscript.exe running a .vbs script out of Downloads, Temp, AppData, Public, or ProgramData — the exact pattern Cato calls out for Poisson's sandbox-evasion stager that decrypted the PowerShell loader. Tier alerting given the script-from-staging-folder combo is rarely legitimate. Rationale: Cato's hunt list: 'wscript.exe running .vbs files out of user staging folders.' The article also notes the stager had a 'sandbox-evasion delay' before decrypting the PowerShell loader — narrowing path-prefix to Downloads/Temp/AppData covers Poisson's drop spots without firing on legitimate GPO logon scripts in System32 or NETLOGON.
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1204.002 T1497.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vendor installer that drops a one-off .vbs cleanup script to %TEMP%
  • Adobe/Citrix uninstaller using a VBScript in ProgramData
  • Legacy ERP/accounting client launching a per-user .vbs from AppData
  • User opening an email-attached invoice (still suspicious — likely a true positive in disguise)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","installer.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("services.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: capture the .vbs file and the parent process — was it Outlook, browser, archive utility (WinRAR/7z), or a service? Decode the VBScript looking for the AES/XOR-decrypted PowerShell second stage Cato describes. Contain: kill wscript.exe tree, quarantine the .vbs file and its source archive, isolate the host. Hunt: pivot on the file SHA256, parent-process tree (was it spawned by a browser/mail client?), and any subsequent PowerShell → .NET in-memory loader spawns on the same host within 1h.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".vbs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Pictures\", @"\Music\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where AccountType =~ "User"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".vbs"
| where CommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

powercfg disabling standby/hibernate to keep host harvest-ready AIActions on Objectives High
Detects powercfg.exe being used to set standby-timeout, hibernate-timeout, monitor-timeout or disk-timeout to 0 — Poisson's trick to prevent the machine sleeping so the local-file keylogger never pauses and he could hand-fetch the keystroke logs. Rationale: Cato's hunt list ends with 'powercfg standby-timeout changes that keep machines awake' — this is the literal article string. Combining standby-timeout/hibernate-timeout/-h off with a zero/off value is the operator-specific shape; powercfg called any other way (e.g. /list, /query) doesn't trip.
ATT&CKT1056.001 T1112 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk script that disables sleep on conference-room/kiosk machines
  • Visual Studio installer toggling sleep during long compiles
  • Backup software (Veeam, Acronis) pinning the host awake during a job window
  • Power management GPO push from SCCM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","veeam.backup.shell.exe","sccm.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("services.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: who is the AccountName — a sysadmin or a regular user? Pull DeviceFileEvents for new files matching keylogger patterns (*.log/*.txt being appended-to-only by a Python or rundll32 process) and DeviceProcessEvents for python.exe / pythonw.exe spawning from non-standard paths. Contain: revert powercfg ('powercfg -change standby-timeout-ac 20'), isolate the host pending IR. Hunt: across the org for the same powercfg → keylogger file-write pair within 24h and for python.exe processes with PIDs that persist across logon/logoff.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "powercfg.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("standby-timeout","hibernate-timeout","monitor-timeout","disk-timeout","-change","/change","-setacvalueindex","-setdcvalueindex","-h off","/h off")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\s|-)0(\b|$)" or ProcessCommandLine has " off"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where AccountType =~ "User"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\powercfg.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("standby-timeout","hibernate-timeout","monitor-timeout","disk-timeout","-change","/change","-h off")
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s0(\b|$)" or CommandLine has " off"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: powercfg Disables Standby/Hibernate to Keep Host Awake

description: powercfg.exe invoked with standby-timeout / hibernate-timeout / monitor-timeout / disk-timeout set to 0 (or -h off) — Poisson's anti-sleep technique to keep the local-file keylogger harvesting continuously.

Logon-trigger scheduled task at HIGHEST privileges launching script interpreter AIInstallation High
Detects schtasks /Create or PowerShell Register-ScheduledTask creating a task with /SC ONLOGON and /RL HIGHEST that runs a script interpreter (powershell/pwsh/wscript/cscript/mshta/rundll32/regsvr32) — Poisson's pinning technique for at-every-logon highest-privilege persistence. Rationale: Cato's hunt list directly: 'scheduled tasks set to the highest privileges that launch script interpreters.' Three required tokens (Create + HIGHEST + ONLOGON) plus an interpreter payload are vanishingly rare in legitimate management tooling — GPO-deployed tasks typically use SYSTEM, not /RL HIGHEST from a user context.
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547 T1078.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • RMM agent (NinjaOne/Datto) registering a logon healthcheck task
  • Citrix/VMware EUC client provisioning script
  • Custom IT logon banner script deployed by a sysadmin
  • Java auto-update logon trigger
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","agent.exe","ninjarmm.exe","datto.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("services.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: dump the created task XML (`schtasks /Query /TN <name> /XML`), capture the script payload, decode any base64 / -EncodedCommand inside. Contain: delete the task (`schtasks /Delete /TN <name> /F`), revoke and re-test the user account, quarantine any payload files referenced. Hunt: pull all Security 4698 events on the host for the last 60d, cross-reference with DeviceFileEvents for the task's Action path, and search the org for tasks with the same name, author, or payload SHA256.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Create","/CREATE","-Create")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/RL HIGHEST","/RL Highest","-RunLevel Highest")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/SC ONLOGON","/SC OnLogon","ONLOGON","-Trigger")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("powershell","pwsh","wscript","cscript","mshta","rundll32","regsvr32",".vbs",".js",".ps1","cmd.exe /c","cmd /c")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where AccountType =~ "User"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/Create","-Create")
| where CommandLine has "HIGHEST"
| where CommandLine has "ONLOGON"
| where CommandLine has_any ("powershell","pwsh","wscript","cscript","mshta","rundll32","regsvr32",".vbs",".ps1")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

authorized_keys file write on Windows host (SSH key persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects creation or modification of `authorized_keys` under any user `.ssh\` directory or under `%ProgramData%\ssh\` — the file Poisson populated to make his key-based SSH reentry persistent. Tier alerting because authorized_keys writes on a Windows endpoint are nearly always operator-grade. Rationale: The article describes Poisson setting up 'key-based SSH' as the reentry path that survived the C2 takedown — the persistence anchor is the authorized_keys file. On Windows the canonical paths are `%USERPROFILE%\.ssh\authorized_keys` and `%ProgramData%\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys`; either being written by anything other than the user's interactive ssh-keygen flow is suspicious.
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1021.004 T1078.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer setting up SSH access to a GitHub repo and writing their own pubkey
  • IT staff bootstrapping an Ansible/SaltStack control node
  • Visual Studio Code Remote-SSH key copy during initial setup
  • User running ssh-copy-id from WSL
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ssh-keygen.exe","notepad.exe","code.exe","explorer.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","pwsh.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: read the authorized_keys file contents — capture every pubkey present and the comments/notes. Pull DeviceLogonEvents for successful SSH inbound logons referencing those keys in the last 30d. Contain: delete the offending lines (or the file), restart sshd, rotate the local user password, force expire any current SSH sessions. Hunt: across the org for authorized_keys writes whose ActingProcess is not ssh-keygen/notepad/code; correlate with Tailscale and OpenSSH-install events on the same host within 7d.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "authorized_keys"
   or FolderPath endswith @"\.ssh\authorized_keys"
   or FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\ssh\"
   or FolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\.ssh\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "authorized_keys"
   or TargetFilePath endswith @"\.ssh\authorized_keys"
   or TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\ssh\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SSH authorized_keys File Written on Windows Host
id: 0df8cf12-9faf-4f80-faec-8fc1edfdf70a
description: Creation/modification of an OpenSSH authorized_keys file on a Windows endpoint — the persistence step Poisson used to lock in key-based SSH reentry.
references:

  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
