| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.object_category="bucket" All_Changes.action="created" (All_Changes.command="storage.buckets.create" OR All_Changes.command="google.storage.v1.Storage.CreateBucket") by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.object, All_Changes.dest, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.vendor_account, All_Changes.vendor_product | `drop_dm_object_name("All_Changes")` | rename object as bucket_name | where match(lower(bucket_name), "vertex-staging-(us|europe|asia|northamerica|southamerica|me-|africa-)") OR match(lower(bucket_name), "-vertex-staging-") | rex field=bucket_name "(?<embedded_project>[^-]+(?:-[^-]+)*)-vertex-staging-(?<region>.+)$" | rex field=user "service-(?<caller_project_num>\d+)@gcp-sa-aiplatform" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | table firstTime, lastTime, user, embedded_project, region, bucket_name, vendor_account, src
Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK install (<1.148.0 - Pickle in the Middle exposure) AIInstallation High
Catches installation or invocation of the google-cloud-aiplatform Python SDK at any version before 1.148.0 — the release that added bucket-ownership verification in Model.upload(). Versions 1.139.0-1.147.x (and the partial-fix 1.144.0-1.147.x with uuid4 randomisation alone) all remain exposed to the bucket-squatting hijack. Sweeps notebooks, CI runners, training pipelines, and production serving images. Rationale: References the exact package name 'google-cloud-aiplatform' and the exact patch boundary versions 1.144.0 (partial fix) and 1.148.0 (complete ownership-check fix) called out in the article. The regex range 1.(1[0-3][0-9]|14[0-7]) precisely encodes the vulnerable window the article describes (1.139.0-1.147.x).
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Reproducible-build CI jobs deliberately pinning a historic SDK version for regression testing
  • Customer-shipped notebooks bundled with Vertex AI SDK 1.140-ish that haven't been refreshed yet
  • pip's resolver downgrading google-cloud-aiplatform because of a transitive version constraint
  • Vendor-supplied container images (training images, MLOps platforms) that haven't released a rebuild
  • Air-gapped / disconnected dev workstations not pulling latest from PyPI
Suppression filter
// Suppress reproducibility test hosts and known-vendor base images
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("ci-repro-","vendor-base-image","legacy-mlops-"))
   and not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("docker.exe","podman.exe") and DeviceName has "build-agent")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull the requirements.txt / pyproject.toml / Pipfile.lock or container image manifest that produced the flagged version. Determine whether this is a production-deployment host or a developer workstation. For workstations, upgrade is sufficient; for serving / training pipelines, this is an active hijack risk. 2. Contain: Force-pin google-cloud-aiplatform>=1.148.0 in the project's dependency manifest and rebuild the affected images. As an immediate compensating control, set `aiplatform.init(staging_bucket='gs://<bucket-you-own>')` in all Model.upload code paths so the SDK's predictable-name logic is never reached. 3. Hunt: Pivot to GCP storage.buckets.create and storage.objects.create logs for any '*-vertex-staging-*' bucket touched by Vertex AI service agents in your project over the last 90 days. Inspect any uploaded .pkl/.joblib model file size and SHA — if the bytes differ from your training output, you have a confirmed swap and should treat the Vertex AI service-agent OAu
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe")
| extend FullCmd = strcat(tostring(ProcessCommandLine), " ", tostring(InitiatingProcessCommandLine))
| where FullCmd has "google-cloud-aiplatform" or FullCmd has "google-vertex-ai"
| extend SdkVersion = extract(@"google-cloud-aiplatform(?:[=<>~]=|@)?\s*(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, FullCmd)
| where isnotempty(SdkVersion)
| extend Parts = split(SdkVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(Parts[0]), Minor = toint(Parts[1])
| where Major == 1 and Minor < 148
| extend PatchState = case(Minor < 144, "unpatched", Minor >= 144 and Minor < 148, "partial-fix-only", "unknown")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, SdkVersion, PatchState, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\pip.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pip3.exe"
    or NewProcessName endswith "\\python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\python3.exe"
    or NewProcessName endswith "\\uv.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\poetry.exe"
| where CommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform" or CommandLine has "google-vertex-ai"
| extend SdkVersion = extract(@"google-cloud-aiplatform(?:[=<>~]=|@)?\s*(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, CommandLine)
| where isnotempty(SdkVersion)
| extend Parts = split(SdkVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(Parts[0]), Minor = toint(Parts[1])
| where Major == 1 and Minor < 148
| extend PatchState = case(Minor < 144, "unpatched", Minor >= 144 and Minor < 148, "partial-fix-only", "unknown")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine, SdkVersion, PatchState
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects pip/uv/poetry installation or invocation pinning google-cloud-aiplatform to any 1.x version below 1.148.0. Versions 1.139.0-1.147.x are exposed to Unit 42's 'Pickle in the Middle' Vertex AI bucket-squatting hijack; 1.144.0-1.147.x carry only the partial uuid4 fix and still lack bucket-ownership verification in Model.upload().

Vertex AI model artifact written to *-vertex-staging-* bucket outside caller's project AIDelivery High
Hunts the actual hijack moment: a Vertex AI service-agent (or a project's user identity) creating a model object (.pkl, .joblib, saved_model.pb) in a Cloud Storage bucket whose name matches the predictable '*-vertex-staging-*' pattern AND whose owning project differs from the caller's project. This is the cross-tenant write that the patched SDK 1.148.0 ownership check is designed to block. Rationale: Targets the specific exploitation primitive named in the article: the SDK uploads the model to a 'project-vertex-staging-region' bucket without checking ownership. The 'embedded project ID in the bucket name != caller's GCP project' condition encodes precisely what the v1.148.0 fix added. Object-type filter (.pkl/.joblib/saved_model) anchors on the article's call-out that 'Many Python ML models are saved with pickle or joblib, which can run code when a file is loaded.'
ATT&CKT1537 T1550.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Multi-project Vertex AI deployment where a central 'ml-platform' project's service agent legitimately writes to staging buckets in tenant project IDs (verify the platform pattern is approved)
  • VPC Service Controls or org-level shared staging bucket intentionally outside the caller's project boundary
  • Migrations / DR scenarios where a Vertex AI job is re-pointed at a backup staging bucket in another project
  • Vendor-supplied Vertex AI pipelines that use a shared customer-data staging area
Suppression filter
// Suppress org-approved multi-project ML-platform pattern
| where not (CallerProject in ("ml-platform-prod","ml-platform-staging") and EmbeddedProject startswith "tenant-")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Verify the destination bucket's owning project is NOT under your org's GCP organization (gcloud projects describe <embedded_project>). If unknown / external, treat as confirmed hijack. Pull the bucket's IAM policy — squat buckets typically have public or attacker-controlled IAM bindings. 2. Contain: Immediately revoke OAuth tokens for the Vertex AI service agent (service-<num>@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com) in the calling project; suspend all in-flight Model.upload / Endpoint.deploy operations; force google-cloud-aiplatform>=1.148.0. File abuse report for the squat bucket. 3. Hunt: Pull aiplatform.googleapis.com Model.upload + Endpoint.deploy audit logs for the affected service-agent over the last 30 days — every model object in the squat bucket may have been swapped. Inspect Vertex AI Endpoint logs and BigQuery jobs.* for the service-agent's tokenacross other tenant projects (Unit 42's note that the stolen token was not scoped to the compromised deployment).

Race-condition pickle swap: rapid object overwrite in Vertex AI staging bucket within 5s AIExploitation High
Detects the model-swap moment of Pickle in the Middle: the same object path inside a '*-vertex-staging-*' bucket receives two storage.objects.create / update events within a 5-second window where the writers are different principals (victim service agent uploading the model, then attacker overwriting it). Unit 42 measured 2.5s between victim upload and Vertex AI read; their PoC swap completed in 1.4s. Rationale: Encodes the exact temporal signature called out in the article: '2.5 seconds between the victim's upload and Vertex AI reading the file' and 'PoC swap completed in 1.4 seconds.' A second write to the same '*-vertex-staging-*/...(pkl|joblib|saved_model)' object by a different principal inside that 5-second envelope has no legitimate analog — Vertex AI normally writes the model once and reads it once.
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vertex AI training pipeline re-running and overwriting its own checkpoint within seconds (same principal — should be excluded by the principal-mismatch clause)
  • Multi-part upload completion races where two API calls land within the window (verify by checking if writers differ by service account)
  • Legitimate retry logic in customer training code overwriting a partial upload
  • Backup / replication tooling mirroring objects between buckets in near-real time
Suppression filter
// Drop same-principal retries even when they hit the 5s window
| where FirstWriter != SecondWriter
   and not (FirstWriter matches regex @"service-\d+@gcp-sa-aiplatform" and SecondWriter matches regex @"service-\d+@gcp-sa-aiplatform" and extract(@"service-(\d+)@",1,FirstWriter) == extract(@"service-(\d+)@",1,SecondWriter))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Inspect both write events' generation IDs (gs://bucket/object?generation=N) and SHA256 hashes if available — different bytes confirm a swap, identical bytes is likely a benign retry. Identify the two principals; one should be the Vertex AI service agent (service-<num>@gcp-sa-aiplatform), the other should be unexpected. 2. Contain: Immediately halt the targeted Vertex AI Endpoint deployment / training job (the malicious pickle has not yet been deserialised if you catch this in time). Revoke the affected service-agent OAuth tokens. Add a Vertex AI org policy blocking Model.upload to any bucket outside an approved allow-list. 3. Hunt: Pull every aiplatform.googleapis.com Endpoint.predict and CustomJob log for the affected project for the last 7 days — if a swap completed undetected, you must assume tenant-wide token compromise (article: 'token was not limited to the compromised deployment ... could access other model artifacts in the same Google-managed tenant project, BigQuery
// Requires Defender for Cloud Apps GCP connector with GCS data-access logs
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Cloud Platform","Google Cloud Storage")
| where ActionType has_any ("storage.objects.create","storage.objects.update","Upload object")
| extend Raw = parse_json(tostring(RawEventData))
| extend ResourceName = tolower(tostring(Raw.protoPayload.resourceName))
| extend Bucket = extract(@"buckets/([^/]+)/objects/", 1, ResourceName)
| extend ObjPath = extract(@"objects/(.+)$", 1, ResourceName)
| extend Principal = tostring(Raw.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail)
| where Bucket has "-vertex-staging-"
| where ObjPath matches regex @"(?i)\.(pkl|pickle|joblib|pb|h5|onnx|safetensors)$" or ObjPath has "saved_model"
| sort by Bucket asc, ObjPath asc, Timestamp asc
| serialize
| extend PrevTime = prev(Timestamp,1), PrevPrincipal = prev(Principal,1), PrevBucket = prev(Bucket,1), PrevObj = prev(ObjPath,1)
| where Bucket == PrevBucket and ObjPath == PrevObj
| extend DeltaSec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, PrevTime)
| where DeltaSec between (0 .. 5) and Principal != PrevPrincipal
| project Timestamp, Bucket, ObjPath, DeltaSec, FirstWriter=PrevPrincipal, SecondWriter=Principal, IPAddress, CountryCode
| order by Timestamp desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

ClickFix Campaigns Expand Malware Delivery With New Loaders and Fake Update Lures

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 18 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged multiple ClickFix campaigns that deliver three malware loaders called BabaDeda Loader, Lorem Ipsum Loader, and Potemkin, per independent reports from Morphisec, BlueVoyant, and Huntress, respectively. Attacks involving BabaDeda Loader, observed in April 2026, have targeted education and financial organizations. "Earlier BabaDeda activity was known for

Exploitation. Potemkin loader victim UUID marker file (hyper-v.ver) in LOCALAPPDATA AIInstallation High
Hunts for the creation of the file hyper-v.ver in %LOCALAPPDATA%, which the Potemkin loader (Huntress, May 2026) writes once per host as its victim-identifier and beacon UUID. The filename masquerades as a Hyper-V artifact but has no legitimate Microsoft product that drops it here. Rationale: The filename %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver is explicitly named in the Huntress writeup quoted in the article as Potemkin's per-victim UUID file. It is unique enough to drive alerting on first sighting.
ATT&CKT1564 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom Hyper-V management script written by an admin storing state in LOCALAPPDATA (very uncommon path)
  • Penetration-testing tools or red-team frameworks reusing the Potemkin naming convention
  • An internal asset-inventory tool dropping a similarly-named file (verify by sha256/parent process)
  • Security researchers detonating Potemkin samples in a non-isolated environment
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","setup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the file's full path + SHA256 + the InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine. Confirm the contents are a random UUID-shaped string (not legitimate Hyper-V state). 2. Contain: isolate the host with Defender live-response, kill the initiating process tree, and quarantine the writing binary (often a Potemkin MSI- or HTA-launched x64 binary). 3. Hunt: on the same host pivot DeviceNetworkEvents for the prior 24h looking for dictionary-style DGA domains; on AlertEvidence/DeviceProcessEvents look for sibling msiexec.exe → mshta.exe chains and EtherRAT/RMMProject follow-on activity. Sweep enterprise-wide for the same filename.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "hyper-v.ver"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "hyper-v.ver"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256

Lorem Ipsum Loader — outdated Node.js 7.10.1 spawned from user-writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts for execution of Node.js 7.10.1 (a 2017 release) from non-standard locations, which the BlueVoyant-tracked Lorem Ipsum Loader bundles in its ClickFix ZIP to run JS-based payloads while evading modern AMSI/EDR script telemetry. A modern enterprise should not be running Node 7.x at all, let alone out of AppData or Temp. Rationale: BlueVoyant explicitly noted the loader uses Node.js v7.10.1 (released 2017) to execute JS payloads from the dropped ZIP. Node 7.x in 2026 is a strong out-of-place signal; combining with non-default install paths keeps FPs to dev workstations only.
ATT&CKT1218 T1059.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Electron-based desktop apps (Slack, VS Code, GitHub Desktop) shipping a bundled node.exe inside AppData
  • Developers using nvm-windows (installs Node into %APPDATA%\nvm)
  • Build tools or CI runners that extract Node to a temp directory before invoking it
  • npx/yarn ad-hoc execution from a project under Downloads
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","slack.exe","github desktop.exe","discord.exe","electron.exe") or FolderPath has @"\nvm\")
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the SHA256 + ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion. If version starts with 7.10 it's a near-certain hit; pull the cmdline to identify the JS file being executed (usually a path inside the ClickFix-dropped ZIP). 2. Contain: kill the node.exe process tree, quarantine the extracted ZIP and any sibling DLLs (mscoree.dll/msvcp140.dll dropped for side-load), and isolate the host. 3. Hunt: pivot DeviceFileEvents for the parent ZIP (look for a recent Edge or browser-spawned .zip download), DeviceImageLoadEvents for non-system32 mscoree.dll/msvcp140.dll loads, and DeviceNetworkEvents for callbacks to social-network-hosted profiles that Lorem Ipsum uses as dead-drop C2 resolvers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion startswith "7.10"
    or (FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
        and not (FolderPath has @"\Program Files\nodejs\" or FolderPath has @"\Program Files (x86)\nodejs\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe" or TargetProcessName has "node.exe"
| extend ImagePath = coalesce(TargetProcessName, ActingProcessName), Cmd = coalesce(TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where (ImagePath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\"))
    and not (ImagePath has @"\Program Files\nodejs\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ImagePath, Cmd, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outdated Node.js Executed From User-Writable Path (Lorem Ipsum Loader)

BabaDeda Storage Crypter external payload container (List.Control.dat) AIInstallation High
Hunts for the file List.Control.dat dropped or read by an unrelated host binary — the Morphisec-named Storage Crypter component of BabaDeda Loader uses files of this shape as the externally-stored, encrypted payload container that is decoded only moments before in-memory execution. Rationale: Morphisec's writeup quoted in the article names List.Control.dat as the externally-stored payload container the Storage Crypter reads to reconstruct DanaBot/SectopRAT in memory. Filename is article-unique and high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1027.013 T1140 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate app accidentally sharing the filename (none known)
  • Internal IR/forensics team replaying a BabaDeda sample
  • Security vendor labs detonating BabaDeda in a corporate sandbox
  • An automated build pipeline producing a similarly-named artifact (investigate the writer's signing)
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the file's full path, SHA256 and the writing process. Inspect bytes — Storage Crypter containers are encrypted, so high-entropy non-PE content with a small (≤2 KB) header is the tell. 2. Contain: isolate the host, quarantine List.Control.dat and the side-loaded application package it lives alongside (the visible legitimate-looking installer), kill the parent process tree. 3. Hunt: enterprise-wide sweep for any other *.Control.dat or *.dat in the same folder; pivot DeviceImageLoadEvents for non-system DLLs loaded out of that folder (side-load chain); on DeviceNetworkEvents check svchost.exe network connections immediately after the read (BabaDeda injects into svchost).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "List.Control.dat"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "List.Control.dat"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername

Lorem Ipsum DLL side-load — mscoree.dll/msvcp140.dll from user-writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the BlueVoyant-documented Lorem Ipsum Loader persistence/execution step: a benign signed host binary loads a malicious mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll planted in the same directory, which then decodes and runs the embedded loader payload. Detection scopes the image load to non-Microsoft directories so genuine .NET / VC++ runtime loads are excluded. Rationale: BlueVoyant named these two DLLs as the side-load vehicles for the Lorem Ipsum Loader chain. Filtering image-load events to user-writable directories cleanly separates the side-load from billions of legitimate runtime loads out of System32/WinSxS.
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable .NET apps in Downloads or AppData that bundle their own VC++ runtime DLLs
  • SCCM/Intune package staging directories under ProgramData
  • Game launchers (Steam, Epic) installing prerequisite VC++ redistributables into a non-Program-Files path
  • Developer build outputs in a user folder with locally-staged dependencies
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Microsoft Corporation","Valve","Epic Games","Adobe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Steam\", @"\Epic Games\", @"\Adobe\"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the loaded DLL's SHA256 + signer; legitimate mscoree.dll/msvcp140.dll are Microsoft-signed and identical-hash across hosts. An unsigned or odd-signer copy in AppData is the hit. 2. Contain: kill the host process, quarantine the planted DLL plus the legit signed loader binary in the same folder (the bait), isolate the host. 3. Hunt: pivot on the folder — look for a ZIP/MSI that recently dropped both files; check DeviceProcessEvents for the parent's parent (often node.exe 7.10.1 from the Lorem Ipsum chain, or msiexec.exe → mshta.exe for Potemkin); enterprise-wide grep for the same SHA256 on other hosts.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("mscoree.dll", "msvcp140.dll")
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\", @"\Windows\WinSxS\", @"\Windows\Microsoft.NET\", @"\Windows\assembly\", @"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\"))
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\PerfLogs\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("mscoree.dll", "msvcp140.dll")
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\", @"\Windows\WinSxS\", @"\Windows\Microsoft.NET\", @"\Windows\assembly\", @"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\"))
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\PerfLogs\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Side-Loaded mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll from User-Writable Path (Lorem Ipsum)
id: 6b9f3a40-2d1e-4a87-b35c-7c8a92e1f0d4
status: experimental
description: Detects mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll loaded from AppData/Temp/Public/ProgramData rather than Windows runtime directories, matching the Lorem Ipsum Loader's BlueVoyant-documented side-load chain.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/clickfix-campaigns-expand-malware.html
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_dll:
    ImageLoaded|endswith:
      - '\mscoree.dll'
      - '\msvcp140.dll'
  selection_userpath:
    ImageLoaded|contains:
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Users\Public\'
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
  filter_legit:
    ImageLoaded|contains:
      - '\Windows\System32\'
      - '\Windows\SysWOW64\'
      - '\Windows\WinSxS\'
      - '\Windows\Microsoft.NET\'
      - '\Program Files\'
  condition: selection_dll and selection_userpath and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Portable .NET applications shipping their own VC++ runtime (uncommon for these two DLLs)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 (@ImageLoaded:(*\\mscoree.dll OR *\\MSCOREE.DLL OR *\\MSCoree.dll) OR @ImageLoaded:(*\\msvcp140.dll OR *\\MSVCP140.DLL OR *\\Msvcp140.dll)) (@ImageLoaded:(*\\AppData\\* OR *\\appdata\\* OR *\\Temp\\* OR *\\Public\\* OR *\\Downloads\\* OR *\\ProgramData\\*)) -@ImageLoaded:(*\\Windows\\System32\\* OR *\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\* OR *\\Windows\\WinSxS\\* OR *\\Windows\\Microsoft.NET\\* OR *\\Program?Files\\*)
#event_simpleName=ImageHash (TargetFileName=/\\mscoree\.dll$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\msvcp140\.dll$/i)
| regex("\\\\(AppData|Temp|Public|Downloads|ProgramData|PerfLogs)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT regex("\\\\(System32|SysWOW64|WinSxS|Microsoft\\.NET|Program Files)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="mscoree.dll" OR Processes.process_name="msvcp140.dll") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where NOT (like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\System32\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\WinSxS\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\Microsoft.NET\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Program Files\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Program Files (x86)\\%"))
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="mscoree.dll" OR Processes.process_name="msvcp140.dll") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where NOT (like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\System32\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\WinSxS\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Windows\\Microsoft.NET\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Program Files\\%") OR like(process_path,"%\\Program Files (x86)\\%"))
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
ClickFix Run-dialog paste: explorer.exe spawning PowerShell/mshta with web-fetch AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the ClickFix initial-access vector that is the common starting point across all three families in the article (BabaDeda, Lorem Ipsum, Potemkin). The user is socially-engineered into pasting an attacker-supplied command into the Win+R Run dialog, which produces an explorer.exe-parented powershell.exe / mshta.exe / cmd.exe with a web-fetch or in-memory-execution flag. Rationale: The article opens with 'a ClickFix social engineering attack that deceives users into running attacker-supplied PowerShell commands'. Explorer→powershell/mshta with a web-fetch or hidden-window flag is the canonical telemetry shape of a Win+R paste, and it is shared across all three loader families described.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmins running ad-hoc PowerShell one-liners from Win+R
  • IT helpdesk scripts that users paste during support sessions
  • Software installers that legitimately spawn powershell with -WindowStyle Hidden from explorer
  • Browser-launched protocol handlers chaining through explorer (rare)
  • Endpoint management agents using a Win+R-style invocation path
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountName in~ ("helpdesk_svc","sccm_admin") or InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel == "System")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode any base64 / -EncodedCommand. Look for an outbound URL — capture it. Check UserDownloads/UrlClickEvents for a click within the prior 5 minutes on a 'verify you are human' / 'fix the issue' style page. 2. Contain: kill the child and the entire chain (often powershell → curl → second-stage binary), isolate the host, block the URL/IP at proxy/DNS. 3. Hunt: search 7d enterprise-wide for the same parent→child→cmd pattern; pivot DeviceFileEvents for List.Control.dat (BabaDeda), hyper-v.ver (Potemkin), or node.exe v7.10.1 spawns (Lorem Ipsum) to attribute which loader family is in play.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (
    "Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","IEX","Invoke-Expression","DownloadString",
    "FromBase64String","-EncodedCommand","-enc ","-W H","-WindowStyle Hidden",
    "curl ","certutil -urlcache","mshta http","mshta https","bitsadmin /transfer",
    "http://","https://")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "explorer.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe") or TargetProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe")
| extend Cmd = coalesce(TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where Cmd has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ","IEX","Invoke-Expression","DownloadString","FromBase64String","-EncodedCommand","-enc ","-W H","-WindowStyle Hidden","curl ","certutil -urlcache","mshta http","mshta https","bitsadmin /transfer","http://","https://")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, Cmd, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ClickFix Run-Dialog Paste — Explorer Spawning PowerShell/Mshta With Web Fetch
id: 9f7c2a18-4e0b-4c5a-bb02-1d6e7f3a8c52
status: experimental
description: Detects explorer.exe spawning powershell/pwsh/mshta/cmd with a web-fetch, encoded, or hidden-window flag — the canonical ClickFix Win+R copy-paste pattern documented for BabaDeda, Lorem Ipsum, and Potemkin campaigns.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/clickfix-campaigns-expand-malware.html
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1204.004
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\explorer.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
      - 'DownloadString'
      - 'IEX'
      - 'Invoke-Expression'
      - 'FromBase64String'
      - '-EncodedCommand'
      - '-enc '
      - '-W H'
      - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
      - 'curl '
      - 'certutil -urlcache'
      - 'mshta http'
      - 'bitsadmin /transfer'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
  - Admins legitimately using Win+R to run a one-liner
  - IT support scripts that admins copy/paste
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\explorer.exe OR *\\Explorer.exe OR *\\EXPLORER.EXE) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE OR *\\cmd.exe) (@CommandLine:(*Invoke-WebRequest* OR *DownloadString* OR *IEX* OR *Invoke-Expression* OR *FromBase64String* OR *-EncodedCommand* OR *"-enc "* OR *"-W H"* OR *"-WindowStyle Hidden"* OR *"certutil -urlcache"* OR *"mshta http"* OR *"bitsadmin /transfer"*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^explorer\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|mshta|cmd)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(Invoke-WebRequest|DownloadString|IEX|Invoke-Expression|FromBase64String|-EncodedCommand|-enc |-W H|-WindowStyle Hidden|certutil -urlcache|mshta http|bitsadmin /transfer)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="explorer.exe" (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="mshta.exe" OR Processes.process_name="cmd.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where match(process,"(?i)(Invoke-WebRequest|iwr |IEX|Invoke-Expression|DownloadString|FromBase64String|-W(in)?(dow)?Style?\s+H(idden)?|curl |certutil\s+-urlcache|mshta\s+http|bitsadmin\s+/transfer)")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="explorer.exe" (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="mshta.exe" OR Processes.process_name="cmd.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where match(process,"(?i)(Invoke-WebRequest|iwr |IEX|Invoke-Expression|DownloadString|FromBase64String|-W(in)?(dow)?Style?\s+H(idden)?|curl |certutil\s+-urlcache|mshta\s+http|bitsadmin\s+/transfer)")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Potemkin loader chain: msiexec spawning mshta with HTA payload AIInstallation High
Hunts the Huntress-documented Potemkin delivery: an installed MSI package drops and invokes an HTA payload via mshta.exe, which loads the Potemkin x64 loader. The msiexec.exe → mshta.exe lineage with a URL or .hta argument is rare in benign software. Rationale: Huntress described the Potemkin chain as 'installs an MSI package, which then drops a previously undocumented loader codenamed Potemkin via an HTML Application (HTA) payload'. msiexec.exe → mshta.exe lineage is rare in legitimate software and is a high-signal pivot, particularly when paired with the hyper-v.ver UC.
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1218.007 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise software whose MSI installer invokes a configuration HTA as a custom action
  • Citrix or VMware installers that historically used HTA-based wizards
  • Internal LOB application installers that wrap configuration in HTAs
  • Engineering/CAD software with HTA-based licensing dialogs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\Citrix\\", "\\VMware\\", "Receiver.msi", "Horizon"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the mshta.exe command line — it will reference either a local .hta path (look at FileCreatedEvents for that path's writer = the MSI) or a URL. SHA256 the MSI to feed VT/IOC pivots. 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill the mshta and any spawned x64 loader, quarantine the MSI and the .hta artefact, block the URL/IP at egress. 3. Hunt: pivot 24h on the host for follow-on activity — Potemkin then writes %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver (run UC1) and beacons via DGA-derived domains; check DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound 1000-word dictionary-style domain lookups; sweep the org for the same MSI SHA256.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "msiexec.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has "mshta.exe" or TargetProcessName has "mshta.exe"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| extend Cmd = coalesce(TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Cmd, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Potemkin Loader Chain — msiexec.exe Spawning mshta.exe
id: 2c8b4d05-91f3-4a7e-bd23-5e9f1c6a2d83
status: experimental
description: Detects msiexec.exe spawning mshta.exe — the Huntress-documented Potemkin loader delivery chain in which an MSI package drops and executes an HTA payload that loads the x64 loader.
references:

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^msiexec\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\mshta\.exe$/i

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071

DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteIP in ("95.163.152.190", "91.92.243.161") or RemoteUrl has_any ("malicious.site")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["95.163.152.190", "91.92.243.161"]);

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Actions on Objectives

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Hunt for vLLM versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-48746 (>=0.3.0, <0.22.0) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] vLLM CVE-2026-48746 auth bypass via Host header URL injection on /v1/* · [LLM] vLLM auth probe-then-bypass: 401/403 followed by 200 on /v1/* from same source
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] vLLM /v1/* successful response (200/201) following Host-header bypass attempt
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
vLLM CVE-2026-48746 auth bypass via Host header URL injection on /v1/* AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests to vLLM OpenAI-compatible /v1/* endpoints where the Host header contains URL special characters (`/`, `?`, or `..`) used to manipulate starlette's URL reconstruction in AuthenticationMiddleware. The article identifies this as the primary exploitation vector: an attacker embeds path/query characters in Host so url_path.removeprefix(root_path) does not begin with `/v1`, skipping the verify_token() check while FastAPI routing still dispatches to the real /v1 endpoint. Rationale: Article explicitly states: 'attacker to include special URL characters such as / or ? in the Host: header'. RFC 7230 Host values are domain[:port] or IP[:port] — `/`, `?`, or `..` are never valid in a conforming Host header, so this is high-fidelity. Default vLLM port 8000 narrows scope further. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised pen-test / bug-bounty researchers probing this exact CVE
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Burp) running CVE-2026-48746 plugins
  • Developer testing the bypass on a staging instance after reading the GHSA
  • Misconfigured upstream proxy that forwards the original Request-URI as a Host override (extremely rare)
  • Security training / CTF lab environments hosting intentionally vulnerable vLLM
Suppression filter
and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Burp", "nuclei", "ZAP") and SrcIpAddr !in (dynamic(["<internal-scanner-IPs>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target IP/host is actually a vLLM instance (default port 8000, look for vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server process). Pull the full request — Host, path, User-Agent, response code. Check vllm package version via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory or pip list. 2) Contain: if vulnerable (vllm >=0.3.0 <0.22.0) and exposed beyond an RFC-conforming proxy, upgrade to >=0.22.0 immediately or front the instance with nginx/Cloudflare to strip the malformed Host. If active 200 responses confirmed, rotate VLLM_API_KEY. 3) Hunt: correlate same source IP to other vLLM endpoints (UC2/UC3), pull all /v1/chat/completions and /v1/completions prompts from same IP/window to assess data extraction, check for downstream LLM-prompt-injection follow-ups against the model.
// Defender XDR has limited HTTP-header visibility; this is a coarse pivot on inbound connections to vLLM's default port. Pair with WAF/uvicorn logs for primary detection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort in (8000, 80, 443, 8080)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("vllm.entrypoints.openai", "vllm serve", "vllm.entrypoints")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, LocalPort, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Hits desc
// Targets WAF / nginx / IIS / vLLM-uvicorn logs forwarded as web sessions. Article: starlette URL.scope rebuild lets `/` or `?` in Host header bypass AuthenticationMiddleware on /v1/*.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/v1/" or HttpHostName has_any ("/", "?", "..")
| where HttpHostName matches regex @"[/?]|\.\."
| extend cve = "CVE-2026-48746"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, EventProduct, cve
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: vLLM CVE-2026-48746 Host Header URL Injection on /v1/*
id: 8e2f6c4a-1d3b-4e57-9a8e-2f3b7c5d4e91
status: experimental
description: Detects HTTP requests to vLLM /v1/* endpoints with URL special characters (/, ?, ..) embedded in the Host header — the exploitation pattern for CVE-2026-48746 AuthenticationMiddleware bypass.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6
author: SOC detection engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:

  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1556
  - cve.2026.48746

  category: webserver

  selection_host_special:

      - '?'

falsepositives:
  - Authorised penetration testers / bug bounty researchers scanning for CVE-2026-48746
  - Misconfigured reverse proxy passing original Request-URI as Host header (rare)
level: high

(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:cloudflare OR source:aws.alb) @http.url_details.path:\/v1\/* (@http.url_details.host:*\/*  OR @http.url_details.host:*\?* OR @http.url_details.host:*..* OR @http.headers.host:*\/* OR @http.headers.host:*\?* OR @http.headers.host:*..*)
WEB

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents values(Web.status) as statuses from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/v1/*" AND (Web.site="*/*" OR Web.site="*?*" OR Web.site="*..*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.dest_port Web.site | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval cve="CVE-2026-48746", note="Host header contains URL special chars - possible vLLM AuthenticationMiddleware bypass" | where dest_port=8000 OR dest_port=80 OR dest_port=443 OR dest_port=8080 | sort 0 - lastSeen
vLLM /v1/* successful response (200/201) following Host-header bypass attempt AIInstallation High
Detects successful (2xx) responses on vLLM OpenAI-compatible /v1/* endpoints when the request Host header carries URL special characters — confirmed evidence that CVE-2026-48746 bypass succeeded. Distinguishes bypass attempts (UC1) from completed exploitation by joining on response status. Rationale: Combines the bypass exploitation indicator from UC1 (Host header URL injection) with the success criterion (2xx response). Article: 'allows to use the API without providing the configured VLLM_API_KEY'. A 200 from /v1/chat/completions under these conditions means the attacker has functional, unauthenticated access to the inference endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised exploit validation during red-team engagements
  • Vendor-supplied vulnerability scanner confirming exploitability for a CVSS report
  • Lab/CTF environments deliberately running unpatched vLLM
  • Internal developer reproducing the GHSA PoC on staging
  • Pen-test tooling sending crafted Host headers with vLLM in scope
Suppression filter
and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Burp", "nuclei") and SrcIpAddr !in (dynamic(["<internal-scanner-IPs>", "<pen-test-IPs>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: critical priority — confirmed bypass. Pull the full /v1/chat/completions or /v1/completions request body to see what prompts/data the attacker submitted. Identify which model and what conversation history was exposed. Check vllm version: if <0.22.0 and >=0.3.0, vulnerable. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the vLLM instance offline or front it with an RFC-conforming proxy (nginx) immediately, rotate VLLM_API_KEY, force re-auth on legitimate clients. 3) Hunt: enumerate every other 2xx to /v1/* from same source IP/ASN over 30 days, check for model-extraction patterns (repeated /v1/embeddings or large /v1/completions volumes), search for outbound exfil from the vLLM host to attacker infra, review served model for sensitive system-prompt disclosure.
// Defender XDR cannot read HTTP request headers. This is the closest pivot: vLLM host accepting inbound /v1/* from public IPs while api-key auth is configured (check VLLM_API_KEY env or --api-key flag in command line).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("vllm.entrypoints.openai", "vllm serve")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--api-key", "VLLM_API_KEY")
| project DeviceName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessCreationTime
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
    | where LocalPort in (8000, 80, 443, 8080)
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
) on DeviceName
| summarize InboundConnections = count(), UniqueRemoteIPs = dcount(RemoteIP), Sample = any(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, ProcessCommandLine
| where InboundConnections > 0
| order by UniqueRemoteIPs desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/v1/"
| where HttpHostName matches regex @"[/?]|\.\."
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200", "201")
| extend cve = "CVE-2026-48746", severity = "critical"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpResponseBodyBytes, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vLLM auth probe-then-bypass: 401/403 followed by 200 on /v1/* from same source AIExploitation Medium
Behavioural correlation: source IP that received 401/403 on vLLM /v1/* endpoints subsequently receives 2xx responses on the same endpoints within a short window — without a credential refresh in between. Matches the CVE-2026-48746 exploitation arc where an attacker probes the auth requirement, then crafts the Host-header bypass and succeeds. Rationale: Article describes the bypass as a discovered behaviour — an attacker must first observe the auth requirement (401/403) before crafting the malformed Host header. The temporal 401→200 transition on the same /v1/* endpoint from the same source, without a credential change visible in headers, is a stronger behavioural signal than either status code alone. Combine with UC1/UC2 for confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate client whose API key expired and was rotated mid-session
  • OAuth token-refresh flow where 401 triggers a refresh and the next request succeeds with a new bearer
  • Client retrying after an initial misconfigured Authorization header
  • Load-balanced clients with stale credential cache hitting the instance after rotation
  • Authorised pen-tester running CVE-2026-48746 PoC against a staging vLLM
Suppression filter
| where SampleSuccessHost matches regex @"[/?]|\.\."
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the failing 401/403 request and the subsequent 200 — compare the Authorization header and Host header byte-for-byte. If the Host changed from a normal value to one with `/`, `?`, or `..` while Authorization was absent on the success, the bypass is confirmed. 2) Contain: block source IP at WAF, take vLLM instance offline or place behind nginx, rotate VLLM_API_KEY. 3) Hunt: from confirmed source IPs, search prior 30 days for other internal /v1/* targets, check for lateral probing of other ASGI/starlette apps in the environment (same bug class affects any starlette app trusting URL.scope), correlate against threat-intel for known mass-scanners.
let WindowMinutes = 15m;
let Failures = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/v1/"
    | where HttpStatusCode in ("401", "403")
    | project FailTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, FailUrl = Url;
let Successes = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/v1/"
    | where HttpStatusCode in ("200", "201")
    | project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, SuccessUrl = Url, SuccessHostHdr = HttpHostName;
Failures
| join kind=inner Successes on SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| where SuccessTime between (FailTime .. FailTime + WindowMinutes)
| summarize FailCount = count(), FirstFail = min(FailTime), FirstSuccess = min(SuccessTime), SampleFailUrl = any(FailUrl), SampleSuccessUrl = any(SuccessUrl), SampleSuccessHost = any(SuccessHostHdr) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| extend DelayToBypassSec = datetime_diff('second', FirstSuccess, FirstFail)
| where FailCount >= 1 and DelayToBypassSec between (1 .. 900)
| extend cve = "CVE-2026-48746"
| order by FirstSuccess desc

Hunt for vLLM versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-48746 (>=0.3.0, <0.22.0) AIReconnaissance High
Asset inventory hunt: enumerate hosts running pip:vllm in the vulnerable version range (>=0.3.0 and <0.22.0) so they can be prioritised for patching to 0.22.0+ or fronted with an RFC-conforming reverse proxy. Drives the patch programme before alerting fidelity matters. Rationale: Article explicitly names the vulnerable package range: 'pip:vllm (vuln >= 0.3.0, < 0.22.0)' and tracks as CVE-2026-48746. Defender's TVM data is the cleanest source — the CveId filter is exact. Process-level hunting catches Linux/container instances that may not be in the TVM inventory. Article also notes 'Instances behind an RFC-conforming web server (such as nginx) are not affected' — pair the inventory with internet-facing flag to prioritise. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched but version string not refreshed in TVM cache
  • Vendor-built containers with backported patches (rare in vLLM ecosystem)
  • Test/dev instances intentionally kept on the vulnerable version for QA reproduction
  • Air-gapped instances where exposure is nil regardless of vLLM version
  • Instances already fronted by nginx/Cloudflare — vulnerable but not exploitable per article note
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank the result set by IsInternetFacing/PublicIP — internet-facing vulnerable instances are P1. For each, confirm whether VLLM_API_KEY or --api-key is set (no API key = no auth to bypass, but the model is open anyway). 2) Contain: for P1 hosts, either (a) upgrade vllm to >=0.22.0, or (b) place behind nginx/Cloudflare/AWS ALB which strip malformed Host headers per RFC. Do not rely on api-key alone — that's exactly what the CVE bypasses. 3) Hunt: once inventory is known, deploy UC1/UC2/UC3 as alerting rules scoped to these hosts. Review WAF/proxy logs retroactively for prior Host-header injection attempts against the inventory.

    | extend Major = toint(split(SoftwareVersion, ".")[0])

    | project DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel = "Critical", RecommendedSecurityUpdate = "Upgrade to vllm >= 0.22.0"
)
| join kind=leftouter (

) on DeviceId
| order by DeviceName asc

| extend Priority = case(IsInternetFacing == true, "P1-internet-facing", "P2-internal")
| order by Priority asc, DeviceName asc

Langflow CVE-2026-48519: POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp with embedded Python code AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated exploitation of Langflow's Shareable Playground RCE. The exploit POSTs to /api/v1/build_public_tmp/<flow-id>/flow with a JSON body whose data.nodes[].data.node.template.code.value field carries arbitrary Python — fires on the exact endpoint+payload pattern named in the advisory PoC. Rationale: Hardcoded to the literal endpoint path '/api/v1/build_public_tmp' named in the GHSA advisory body and PoC cURL. POST/PUT-only because the vulnerable code path requires a JSON body with the malicious nodes[].data.node.template.code.value field. Cross-checked with NVD entry for CVE-2026-48519 and the langflow-ai/langflow GitHub release notes for 1.9.1. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5ff-9q35-q26f • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48519 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user accessing a Shareable Playground link they were intentionally given
  • Langflow developer testing flows locally during development
  • Internal QA/load-testing tools exercising the endpoint
  • Browser auto-replays of saved POST requests from devtools session
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys) probing the path for CVE-2026-48519
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientIP in ("<known-admin-ip-1>","<known-admin-ip-2>") and UserAgent has_any ("Mozilla","Chrome","Firefox") and BytesIn < 2048)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full POST body for the matching request and check whether data.nodes[].data.node.template.code.value contains Python builtins (exec, eval, __import__, subprocess, os.system, socket) or shell tokens (touch, curl, wget, bash, /tmp/, /dev/shm). A benign Shareable Playground click sends only stock chat-input wiring. Step 2 (contain): If malicious payload confirmed, block the source IP at the edge, disable the affected public flow (DELETE on the flow's public_id), and isolate the Langflow host pending forensics. If patch is available, upgrade to >1.9.1 immediately. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the Langflow host's outbound network for the next 24h for any new domains/IPs, check /tmp /dev/shm and the Langflow working directory for new files, and grep langflow logs for other public flow IDs hit by the same client_id cookie or source IP.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp" or AdditionalFields has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LangflowHits_IIS = W3CIISLog

    | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP = cIP, UriStem = csUriStem, UriQuery = csUriQuery, Method = csMethod, Status = scStatus, UserAgent = csUserAgent, BytesIn = csBytes;
let LangflowHits_CEF = CommonSecurityLog
