    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DestinationHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, UriStem = RequestURL, UriQuery = RequestContext, Method = RequestMethod, Status = tostring(EventOutcome), UserAgent = RequestClientApplication, BytesIn = ReceivedBytes;
union isfuzzy=true LangflowHits_IIS, LangflowHits_CEF
| extend SuspiciousPayloadSize = iff(BytesIn > 1024, true, false)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow exploit reconnaissance: clustered errors against /api/v1/build_public_tmp AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects burst of HTTP 4xx/5xx responses from the Langflow /api/v1/build_public_tmp endpoint by a single source IP — the failure signature of attackers iterating flow IDs or malformed JSON payloads before landing a working CVE-2026-48519 exploit. Tunable threshold; defaults to >=10 errors per source IP within 10 minutes. Rationale: Pre-RCE recon shape — attackers iterating flow IDs (404), JSON shape (400), or malformed payloads (500) against the literal endpoint path '/api/v1/build_public_tmp' the advisory names. Threshold of 10/10min separates scanner activity from a single user re-clicking a stale share link. Cross-checked NVD CVE-2026-48519 detail and the langflow repository's build_public_tmp route handler. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5ff-9q35-q26f • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48519
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner sweep (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) probing for CVE-2026-48519
  • User repeatedly clicking a Shareable Playground link after the underlying flow was deleted (404 loop)
  • Frontend SPA bug causing a request retry loop against the endpoint
  • WAF blocking legitimate requests and generating 403s in a burst
  • Health-check / monitoring tools probing the endpoint without a valid flow ID
Suppression filter
| where ClientIP !in ("<scanner-ip-1>","<scanner-ip-2>") and UserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","masscan","healthcheck")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Look up the source IP in threat intel (Shodan, AbuseIPDB, internal IOC list) and check what HTTP status codes dominate the burst — pure 404s suggest flow-ID guessing, mixed 400/500 suggests payload fuzzing, pure 403 suggests WAF blocking. Step 2 (contain): If external + non-scanner, block the source IP at the WAF/edge and rate-limit the /api/v1/build_public_tmp path globally. If internal, identify the scanner and exclude the IP from this rule. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the source IP for any successful (HTTP 200) calls to the same endpoint in the surrounding 30 minutes — those are the exploitation attempt that landed. Cross-reference with UC1 (POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp).

Langflow Python runtime spawning shell/subprocess children (post-exploit RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-48519: the Langflow Python worker (uvicorn/gunicorn/python running langflow) spawning sh/bash/cmd or invoking touch/curl/wget/socket-bind. The PoC payload literally runs 'touch /tmp/pwned' via the injected node code, so any non-trivial subprocess from the Langflow runtime is highly suspicious. Rationale: Article PoC literally executes 'touch /tmp/pwned' via the data.nodes[].data.node.template.code.value field — this UC catches that exact payload plus the broader family of shell/network/filesystem children that a Langflow worker has no business spawning. Stacktrace in the advisory confirms langflow runs in a Python interpreter (likely uvicorn/gunicorn), so parent-process filter on those binaries is high-fidelity. Cross-checked langflow Dockerfile in the langflow-ai/langflow repo for default entrypoint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5ff-9q35-q26f • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48519
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow flow with a legitimate ShellTool / BashTool component that intentionally invokes shell commands
  • Container healthcheck script running curl/wget against localhost from inside the Langflow pod
  • Operator exec'ing into the Langflow container to run diagnostics (touch, ls, cat)
  • Langflow's own pip install / package management invoking sh during component installation
  • CI/CD pipeline running smoke tests that invoke Python -> shell from inside a Langflow image build
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("healthcheck","pip install","apt-get","yum install") and Account in~ ("root","langflow","app") and ParentImage has "entrypoint")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the child process command line and the parent's recent network activity. If the child is 'touch /tmp/pwned' or any literal from the advisory's PoC, treat as confirmed exploit. Otherwise check whether the command line matches a known Langflow ShellTool component used in this deployment. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the Langflow host/container, capture memory if feasible, suspend all public_flow IDs (set is_public=false in the DB), and rotate any credentials/API keys the Langflow runtime had access to (LLM API keys, vector DB creds, internal service tokens). Patch to langflow >1.9.1. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep DeviceFileEvents for new files written by the python parent in /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp, and the Langflow working directory in the last 7 days. Sweep outbound network from the Langflow host for new external IPs/domains. Pivot on UC1 (POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp) to identify the originating exploit request and source IP.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","python.exe","uvicorn","gunicorn")
      or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow","build_public_tmp")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","touch","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","chmod","base64")
      or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/pwned","touch /tmp/","touch /dev/shm","bash -i","sh -c","-c \"import os\"","socket.socket","subprocess.Popen","os.system")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspChildren = dynamic(["sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","touch","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","chmod","base64"]);
let SuspCmdTokens = dynamic(["/tmp/pwned","touch /tmp/","touch /dev/shm","bash -i","sh -c","subprocess.Popen","os.system","socket.socket"]);
let WinHits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn") or CommandLine has "langflow"
    | where tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]) in~ (SuspChildren) or CommandLine has_any (SuspCmdTokens)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, ParentImage = ParentProcessName, ChildImage = NewProcessName, ChildCmd = CommandLine;
let AsimHits = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn") or ParentProcessCommandLine has "langflow"
    | where TargetProcessName has_any (SuspChildren) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (SuspCmdTokens)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, ParentImage = ParentProcessName, ChildImage = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine;
union isfuzzy=true WinHits, AsimHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 5 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Security researchers at&nbsp;Zimperium's zLabs&nbsp;have documented a new Android banking trojan, Rokarolla, that targets 217 banking and cryptocurrency apps and packs 137 remote commands. Together, they give an operator near-total control of an infected phone: it lifts lock-screen PINs, reads and sends SMS, rewrites the clipboard to redirect crypto payments, and switches off Google Play

Rokarolla Android banking trojan C2 contact — beralisvc.info AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS resolution or HTTP(S) network traffic to beralisvc.info, the named command-and-control domain for the Rokarolla Android banking trojan documented by Zimperium zLabs in June 2026. The malware is named after this C2 family; any successful resolution from a managed mobile device, BYOD on corporate Wi-Fi, or corporate egress path is a near-certain indicator of an infected Android device performing overlay-credential exfiltration, SMS OTP theft, or accessibility-driven screenshot upload. Rationale: Anchored on the single hard IOC the article names — the C2 domain beralisvc.info — which the malware family is itself named after (Zimperium named it after the C2 servers). Behavioral TTPs in the article (Accessibility abuse, default-SMS-app hijack, overlay credential theft, screenshot-via-Accessibility exfiltration) require mobile-EDR-specific telemetry that isn't part of the standard Defender/Sentinel/Falcon/Datadog schemas in this prompt, so additional UCs would either restate this network IOC or hallucinate column names. One sharp detection beats five generic mobile templates. Cross-checked against The Hacker News, Infosecurity Magazine, and HackRead — all three independent write-ups attribute the campaign to Zimperium zLabs and confirm the C2-naming convention. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-rokarolla-android-malware-steals.html • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/rokarolla-android-banking-trojan/ • https://hackread.com/rokarolla-android-trojan-crypto-and-banking-apps/ • https://zimperium.com/blog/android-bankers-4-campaigns-in-a-row
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1437.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analysis sandbox / detonation VM resolving the IOC after a sample upload
  • Threat intel platform (MISP, OpenCTI, ThreatConnect) running automated enrichment lookups against the published IOC
  • Browser link-unfurling or preview services automatically fetching domain context when SOC analysts share the article in chat
  • SOC engineer manually pinging or curl-checking the domain during this very investigation
  • Mobile DFIR lab triaging a captured device with live C2 still active
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("malware-sandbox-01","ti-detonation-vm","sandbox-android-01","misp-enrichment-host") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","curl","wget.exe","wget","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe","python3") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "misp" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "opencti"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceInfo (OSPlatform, JoinType, LoggedOnUsers) for the resolving device. If Android, identify owner via MDM/Intune and confirm BYOD vs corporate-owned. If Windows/Linux or a known analyst workstation, validate against TI-sandbox/IR-tooling allowlist before escalating. Capture the InitiatingProcessFileName — on Android Defender this surfaces the offending package name. 2) Contain: for confirmed end-user mobile infections, issue Intune retire-and-wipe (factory reset is required; reinstall-only leaves the dropper). Force credential rotation for every banking, crypto-exchange, wallet, email, and SSO account ever used on the device. Sinkhole beralisvc.info and *.beralisvc.info at the corporate resolver and egress firewall. Notify the user's bank fraud team — SMS-OTP capture means recent transactions may be attacker-initiated. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for the prior 14 days for other newly-resolved low-reputation .info/.top/.xyz domains (fallback C2), elevated counts of

Pickle in the Middle – Hijacking Vertex AI Model Uploads for Cross-Tenant RCE

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-06-16 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Unit 42 discovered a Vertex AI Python SDK vulnerability that allows remote code execution via bucket squatting. Read the article for more. The post Pickle in the Middle – Hijacking Vertex AI Model Uploads for Cross-Tenant RCE appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK install (CVE-2026-2473 — pre-1.148.0)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Vertex AI default staging bucket squatting — predictable bucket pattern access · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Pickle in the Middle – Hijacking Vertex AI Model Uploads for Cross-Tenant RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK install (CVE-2026-2473 — pre-1.148.0) AIWeaponization High
Detects installation or invocation of google-cloud-aiplatform Python SDK at versions 1.139.0 through 1.147.x, which silently fall back to an attacker-owned GCS bucket via the deterministic `<project>-vertex-staging-<location>` pattern when no explicit staging bucket is supplied. Catches both first-time installs and runtime use of vulnerable libraries that should be upgraded to ≥1.148.0. Rationale: Pins to the EXACT vulnerable SDK version range disclosed in the Unit 42 article (1.139.0 — 1.147.x; fixed in 1.148.0 released 2026-04-15). The version regex eliminates noise from already-patched installs. Catches both interactive pip installs and CI/CD pipelines pulling pinned vulnerable versions. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://pypi.org/project/google-cloud-aiplatform/#history
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data science teams legitimately running pinned but outdated SDK versions in research notebooks
  • CI/CD pipelines re-installing an old pinned version in lockfiles awaiting upgrade
  • Docker image rebuilds replaying historical pip install commands from cached layers
  • Developers reproducing a known issue against a specific old SDK version for support tickets
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("docker.exe","buildkitd.exe") and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","download","--no-deps"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user and pull the full pip-install context — is this a developer workstation, build agent, or production ML pipeline? Check whether the SDK is actively used (search for `aiplatform.Model.upload` calls in the same project). 2) Contain: force-upgrade google-cloud-aiplatform to ≥1.148.0 in the affected environment; if the host has uploaded models in the last 7 days, treat any default-named staging buckets as suspect and verify ownership via `gcloud storage buckets describe`. 3) Hunt: pivot to GCS audit logs for any bucket matching `<project-id>-vertex-staging-<location>` and confirm the bucket resides in the customer's own project, not an attacker-controlled one. Check Vertex AI Model Registry for models uploaded during the vulnerable window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pip","pip3","python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"google-cloud-aiplatform==1\.(139|140|141|142|143|144|145|146|147)\."
| extend VulnerableVersion = extract(@"google-cloud-aiplatform==(1\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountUpn, VulnerableVersion, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "pip.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "pip3.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "python3.exe"
| where CommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"google-cloud-aiplatform==1\.(139|140|141|142|143|144|145|146|147)\."
| extend VulnerableVersion = extract(@"google-cloud-aiplatform==(1\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, CommandLine)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, SubjectUserName, VulnerableVersion, CommandLine, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vertex AI default staging bucket squatting — predictable bucket pattern access AIDelivery Medium
Hunts GCP audit logs for storage operations on buckets matching the deterministic `<project-id>-vertex-staging-<location>` pattern where the acting identity is NOT the customer's Vertex AI P4SA (`service-<project-num>@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com`) or a known internal pipeline service account. Surfaces both cross-tenant bucket squatting and unexpected writes that could be model-artifact poisoning. Rationale: Targets the exact bucket-name pattern from the article (`staging_bucket_name = project + "-vertex-staging-" + location`). Filtering OUT the legitimate Vertex AI P4SA isolates the access path the attacker would use — either bucket-squatting from a different project or an unexpected internal principal touching the staging bucket. Sigma omitted because this requires aggregation/exclusion logic not expressible as single-event-shape. Falcon/Defender/CloudWatch empty because this is GCP-native telemetry with no Falcon FDR or Microsoft endpoint equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-agents
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1525 T1530
Data sourcesWeb Change
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Customer DevOps service account legitimately reading the staging bucket during pipeline orchestration
  • Terraform/IaC service account creating or auditing the bucket during infra provisioning
  • Cloud Storage Transfer Service or Backup service principals enumerating buckets
  • Internal user using `gcloud storage` CLI for ad-hoc model artifact inspection
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm bucket ownership with `gcloud storage buckets describe gs://<bucket>` — if the project_number doesn't match your project, you've been squatted; treat as confirmed. Inventory any model artifacts already staged there. 2) Contain: immediately delete and recreate the bucket explicitly under your project, then upgrade the SDK to ≥1.148.0 across all clients. Revoke any models uploaded during the vulnerable window from the Vertex AI Model Registry and redeploy from a verified source. 3) Hunt: pull Vertex AI deployment events for the affected region and inspect model artifacts (`gsutil cat gs://<bucket>/.../model.joblib | python -c 'import pickletools; pickletools.dis(...)'`) for `__reduce__` payloads. Check IAM audit logs for any new permissions granted to external principals.
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ServiceName == "storage.googleapis.com"
| extend BucketName = extract(@"projects/_/buckets/([^/]+)", 1, tostring(ResourceName))
| where BucketName matches regex @"-vertex-staging-(us|europe|asia|australia|northamerica|southamerica)"
| extend Principal = tostring(AuthenticationInfo.principalEmail)
| where Principal !endswith "@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Methods=make_set(MethodName), Principals=make_set(Principal), EventCount=count() by BucketName
| order by LastSeen desc
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.serviceName:storage.googleapis.com @protoPayload.resourceName:*-vertex-staging-* -@protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail:*@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com
CLOUD
`gcp_audit_logs` data.protoPayload.serviceName="storage.googleapis.com"
| rex field=data.protoPayload.resourceName "projects/_/buckets/(?<bucket_name>[^/]+)"
| where match(bucket_name, "-vertex-staging-(us|europe|asia|australia|northamerica|southamerica)")
| eval principal=data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail
| where NOT match(principal, "gcp-sa-aiplatform\.iam\.gserviceaccount\.com$")
| stats min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(data.protoPayload.methodName) as methods values(principal) as principals count by bucket_name
| `security_content_ctime(firstSeen)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastSeen)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-2473")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

    category: process_creation

detection:

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
